title: Magnetic materials: which things a magnet pulls, and which it does not

summary.text: This unit is about which materials a magnet pulls. A material is magnetic if a magnet pulls it. Iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Wood, plastic, glass, paper, cloth and stone are not. The big surprise is that most metals are not magnetic either. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are all ignored by a magnet, and so are some steel tumblers. The reason is hidden inside the atoms, where tiny magnets line up in iron but not in brass. A magnet test can show that a thing contains iron. It can never show that a thing is gold. Scientists still cannot predict every new magnetic material.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a fridge magnet holding a drawing on a steel fridge door with an iron nail stuck beside it, on the right the same magnet next to a wooden cupboard door, an aluminium foil ball and a brass key, all untouched, with the magnet looking puzzled.

intro.hook: Try this. Take a fridge magnet to your kitchen. Touch it to a steel spoon, then to a steel tumbler. Both are grey and shiny and called steel. Does the magnet treat them the same?
intro.text: In many kitchens, the answer is no. The spoon grabs the magnet, but the tumbler may not. A magnet will stick to the fridge door, but it will fall off the wooden cupboard door right beside it. So a magnet is choosy. It picks some things and leaves others, and it is not picking by colour or by shine. What is it picking by? This unit is about finding out. You will test thirty or more things and spot a pattern. Then you will meet a surprise that even many grown-ups get wrong.
intro.art: A kitchen counter: a hand holding a fridge magnet over a steel spoon that jumps up to meet it, and over a steel tumbler that does not, with a question mark floating between them.

outcomes: I can say what magnetic and non-magnetic mean. A magnet pulls a magnetic thing, and does not pull a non-magnetic one.
I can predict, test and record which objects a magnet pulls, and sort them into two groups.
I can say the pattern: a magnet pulls iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt, and not every metal is magnetic.
I can explain why two steel things can behave differently, because steel is an alloy and the mixture matters.
I can show that a magnet's pull goes through paper, cloth, plastic and water. I can show that it gets weaker as the gap grows.
I can say what a magnet test can prove and what it cannot, and use a magnet to sort scrap.
I can say, in simple words, why iron is magnetic: tiny magnets inside it line up. I can also give big examples: the Earth's iron core, magnetic bacteria, and a frog floating in a magnet.

terms.meaning: A thing that pulls iron and steel towards it, with no rope or glue. It has this pull all by itself.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge door.
terms.art: A fridge magnet holding a child's drawing on a steel fridge door.

terms.meaning: Pulled by a magnet. Iron and most steel are magnetic.
terms.example: An iron nail jumps towards a magnet. So the nail is magnetic.
terms.art: An iron nail leaping up to a magnet held above it.

terms.meaning: Not pulled by a magnet, or pulled so little that we cannot notice.
terms.example: A wooden spoon, a glass bangle and aluminium foil are all non-magnetic.
terms.art: A magnet held over a wooden spoon, a glass bangle and a foil ball, none moving.

terms.meaning: To pull towards. A magnet attracts magnetic things.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a paper clip. The clip leaps up and sticks.
terms.art: A paper clip jumping up to a magnet with small motion lines.

terms.meaning: The pull that a magnet puts on magnetic things. It works across a small gap, so the magnet need not touch.
terms.example: Hold a magnet just above a paper clip. The clip jumps up before they touch.
terms.art: A magnet above a clip with a gap and faint curved lines between them.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of.
terms.example: A spoon can be made of steel, wood or plastic. Steel, wood and plastic are materials.
terms.art: Three spoons side by side, one steel, one wooden, one plastic.

terms.meaning: A material that is usually shiny, feels cold, and rings when you tap it. Heat and electricity pass easily through metals.
terms.example: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver are metals.
terms.art: A row of metal samples: a nail, a copper wire, foil, a gold ring and a silver coin.

terms.meaning: A grey metal that a magnet pulls strongly. It goes brown and flaky with rust when it stays wet.
terms.example: An old gate, a tawa and a nail may be made of iron.
terms.art: A rusty iron gate with a magnet stuck to one bar.

terms.meaning: Iron with a little carbon mixed in, which makes it much stronger. Most steel is magnetic, but some kinds are not.
terms.example: Train tracks, a bridge, a spoon and an almirah are made of steel.
terms.art: A train track, a steel spoon and an almirah in one row.

terms.meaning: A metal mixed with something else, usually other metals, to give it new properties. Steel, brass and bronze are alloys.
terms.example: Brass is copper mixed with zinc. A magnet ignores brass, because it ignores copper and zinc too.
terms.art: Two metal pots pouring into one mould, with the new metal shining gold.

terms.meaning: A steel that hardly rusts, because another metal called chromium is mixed in. Some kinds also have nickel.
terms.example: Your steel tumbler is probably stainless steel. A magnet may stick to it, or may not.
terms.art: A shiny steel tumbler and katori on a kitchen shelf, with a fridge magnet hovering over each.

terms.meaning: Two metals that a magnet pulls, just like iron. They are much rarer in everyday things.
terms.example: Nickel is in some coins. Cobalt is in some strong magnets and in phone batteries.
terms.art: A silvery coin and a small pile of grey cobalt chunks, with a magnet pulling a pin towards each.

terms.meaning: A natural rock that is already a magnet. It is a form of a dark mineral called magnetite.
terms.example: People found lodestones thousands of years ago, and saw them pull iron.
terms.art: A dark, rough lodestone with iron pins clinging to it.

terms.meaning: Something that keeps happening in your results.
terms.example: Every object that stuck was made of iron or steel. That is a pattern.
terms.art: Two piles of objects, with a glowing line joining all the objects in the stuck pile.

terms.meaning: To guess what will happen before you try, and to have a reason for your guess.
terms.example: I predict the brass key will not stick, because brass is not iron.
terms.art: A child with a thought bubble showing a key and a cross.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A nail, a wooden spoon and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a nail to a speck of iron to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: A tiny bit on the outside of every atom. Each electron spins, and a spinning electron acts like a very tiny magnet.
terms.example: In an iron nail, the tiny magnets from billions of electrons line up in groups. That is why the nail is magnetic.
terms.art: An atom with small spinning balls, each drawn with a tiny arrow.

terms.meaning: A tiny patch inside iron where countless atoms all act like little magnets pointing the same way.
terms.example: A nail is full of domains. A nearby magnet turns many of them to point the same way, so the nail gets pulled.
terms.art: A zoomed picture of a nail, split into patches, each patch full of small arrows pointing one way.

terms.meaning: To turn a magnetic thing into a magnet, at least for a while.
terms.example: Touch a nail to a magnet and it can pick up a paper clip. The nail has been magnetised.
terms.art: A nail touching a magnet and a chain of paper clips hanging from the nail.

terms.meaning: The heat at which a magnetic material stops being magnetic. For iron it is about 770 degrees Celsius. It is named after Pierre Curie, a French scientist.
terms.example: A nail glowing red-hot is above its Curie point, so a magnet no longer pulls it.
terms.art: A glowing red-hot nail next to a magnet that is ignoring it.

terms.meaning: A hard, dark, brittle ceramic made from iron joined with oxygen, mixed with other powders. Most fridge magnets are made of it.
terms.example: A flat black fridge magnet is often ferrite powder held in rubber.
terms.art: A broken piece of dark ceramic magnet beside a flexible fridge magnet sheet.

terms.meaning: Pushed away, very weakly, by a magnet. Almost everything is a little diamagnetic, including water, wood and you.
terms.example: A live frog was floated in the air by a very strong magnet, because the frog is diamagnetic.
terms.art: A small green frog floating calmly in the air inside a large magnet.

terms.meaning: Old metal and broken things that are thrown away. Scrap is melted and made into new things.
terms.example: A kabadiwala buys scrap iron, steel, aluminium and copper.
terms.art: A heap of old pots, pipes and cans.

terms.meaning: A person who buys old paper, bottles and metal from homes, and sells them on to be recycled.
terms.example: The kabadiwala weighs your old newspapers and a broken iron pan, and pays you for them.
terms.art: A man with a hand scale weighing a bundle of newspapers beside a pile of metal.

explanations.definition: A material is magnetic if a magnet pulls it. A material is non-magnetic if a magnet does not pull it, or pulls it too little to notice.
explanations.description: Hold a magnet near a paper clip, and the clip jumps up to meet it. Hold the same magnet near a wooden spoon, and nothing happens. We call the clip magnetic and the spoon non-magnetic. The pull works across a small gap, so the magnet does not need to touch. Be careful with the word. Magnetic means a magnet pulls it. It does not mean it is a magnet. A paper clip is magnetic, but it is not a magnet. It cannot pull other clips by itself, unless a real magnet has just given it some power.
examples: A paper clip is magnetic. It leaps to a magnet.
A plastic comb is non-magnetic. It stays where it is.
A steel almirah door is magnetic. That is why a fridge magnet can hold up a drawing on it.
explanations.art: Three panels: a clip jumping up to a magnet, a plastic comb unmoved, a fridge magnet holding a drawing on a steel door.
explanations.context: This card explains the main word of the whole unit, magnetic, and what it does and does not mean.

explanations.definition: A magnet pulls iron, most kinds of steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not pull wood, plastic, glass, paper, cloth, rubber or stone.
explanations.description: Test enough things and a pattern appears. The things that jump to a magnet are made of iron or steel, or a little nickel or cobalt. Nails, safety pins, paper clips, tawas and almirahs are the usual ones. Everything made of wood, plastic, glass, paper, cloth, rubber or stone is ignored. This works for thousands of everyday objects. Scientists have checked it for hundreds of years. But there are exceptions, and they are the best part of the unit.
examples: Pulled: an iron nail, a safety pin, a paper clip, a steel almirah.
Not pulled: a wooden pencil, a plastic ruler, a glass bangle, a cotton hanky, a stone.
A tin can is steel with a thin coat of tin, so a magnet sticks to it.
explanations.art: Two shelves labelled with a tick and a cross: nails, pins and clips on the tick shelf, and wood, plastic, glass and cloth on the cross shelf.
explanations.context: After testing many things, what is the pattern? This card gives the main answer, which you can check yourself in the Great Magnet Test.

explanations.definition: Only three common metals are magnetic: iron, nickel and cobalt. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, zinc, tin and lead are not.
explanations.description: Many people believe a magnet pulls every metal. It does not. Try an aluminium foil ball, a copper wire, a brass key and a gold ring. They are all shiny metals, and a magnet ignores every one. There are about ninety kinds of natural element. Only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic in an ordinary room. A fourth one, gadolinium, is magnetic only when it is colder than about 20 degrees Celsius. So being a metal is not the secret. Something about iron, nickel and cobalt is special. Later in this unit you will zoom in and find out what.
examples: Aluminium foil and aluminium pressure cookers are not pulled.
A brass diya and a copper lota are not pulled.
A gold ring and a silver anklet are not pulled.
explanations.art: A row of shiny metal things, a foil ball, a copper lota, a brass diya, a gold ring, each with a small cross, and a nail with a tick.
explanations.context: Do magnets pull all metals? This card gives the surprising answer, and explains why shiny does not mean magnetic.

explanations.concept: Steel is a mixture, so steel can differ
explanations.definition: Steel is an alloy, which means a mixture. It is iron with a little carbon. Stainless steel also has chromium, and often nickel. The mixture decides whether a magnet pulls it.
explanations.description: Here is the tumbler puzzle. Most steel is mostly iron, so a magnet pulls it. But the steel in many Indian tumblers, katoris and thalis has a lot of nickel mixed in. In every 100 parts, there may be about 18 parts of chromium and 8 parts of nickel. The nickel changes how the iron atoms sit next to each other. In that new pattern, the iron's tiny magnets do not line up. So the magnet barely pulls. Other stainless steels have chromium but little nickel. They do stick. Pots for induction stoves must be that sticking kind, because the stove works through magnetism. You may also find that a tumbler's bottom sticks but its sides do not. A bent corner may stick a little too, because bending can rearrange the atoms.
examples: A steel almirah, a tawa and many spoons stick to a magnet.
Many tumblers and katoris do not stick, or stick only weakly.
A pan that works on an induction stove always sticks to a magnet.
explanations.art: Two steel katoris with a magnet: one holds the magnet firmly, the other lets it slide off, a magnified circle shows iron atoms in two different patterns.
explanations.context: Why do two steel things behave differently? This card explains the tumbler puzzle from the start of the unit.

explanations.concept: Mixing can switch magnetism on or off
explanations.definition: Mixing metals can make a mixture that behaves nothing like its ingredients. A mix of magnetic metals can lose its magnetism. A mix of non-magnetic metals can gain it.
explanations.description: In 1903, a German scientist called Fritz Heusler made a mixture of copper, manganese and aluminium. None of those three metals is magnetic. But the mixture was. Heusler could not explain it, and nobody could for years. We now know the manganese atoms sit in a special pattern in the mixture. Their tiny magnets line up. It works the other way too. A stainless steel with nickel loses the magnetism that plain iron has. So you cannot work out magnetism by looking at the list of ingredients. You must test.
examples: Heusler's copper, manganese and aluminium mix is magnetic, though none of its metals is.
Alnico is a mixture of aluminium, nickel and cobalt, with iron, used for strong magnets in loudspeakers. Aluminium alone is not magnetic.
Nickel-rich stainless steel is not magnetic, though plain iron is.
explanations.art: A mixing pot with three grey metals going in, a magnet pulling a pin from the finished bar, and a question mark above the pot.
explanations.context: This card shows how mixing metals can give surprises, and why scientists always test instead of guessing.

explanations.concept: Tiny magnets inside: why iron is magnetic
explanations.definition: Inside iron, nickel and cobalt, the tiny magnets of many atoms line up in groups called domains. A nearby magnet turns the domains to point the same way, so the metal is pulled.
explanations.description: Zoom in past anything a microscope can show, and you find atoms. Zoom in further, and you find electrons. Every electron spins, and a spinning electron acts like a very tiny magnet. In most materials, the tiny magnets point every which way, so they cancel out. A wooden spoon has countless tiny magnets, but no pull. In iron, neighbouring atoms make each other point the same way, in patches called domains. A domain has billions and billions of atoms. A nail is full of domains, but they point in different directions, so the nail is not a magnet. Bring a real magnet close, and the domains swing round to match it. Now the nail has a pull of its own, and it is drawn to the magnet. Move the magnet away, and most domains drift back. In hard steel, many stay lined up, which is how steel can become a lasting magnet.
examples: A nail touched to a magnet can pick up paper clips. Pull it away and the clips fall, as the domains drift back.
A steel needle stroked many times with a magnet keeps its pull for a long time.
Hit a magnet hard, or drop it many times, and it weakens. The domains get shaken out of line.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a nail, a patch of metal, domains as coloured patches with arrows, and then the arrows swinging to line up when a magnet arrives.
explanations.context: Why only iron, nickel and cobalt? This card zooms into the atoms to find the answer.

explanations.concept: Why do iron's tiny magnets line up?
explanations.description: You might expect tiny magnets to turn and point opposite ways, like two fridge magnets that snap together. That is not what happens in iron. Something stronger makes neighbours copy each other. The answer needs quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things. It says that electrons find it easier to be near each other when they spin the same way. This rule has no everyday example, and it is not about magnets pulling at all. Scientists agree that this rule exists. They still argue about the best picture of how it works in a real piece of metal.
examples: Iron, nickel and cobalt all have electrons that can line up this way.
Copper and aluminium have electrons that pair up and cancel out instead.

perspectives.who: Werner Heisenberg, a German physicist, in 1928
perspectives.explanation: Each atom keeps its own tiny magnet. Quantum physics makes neighbouring atoms copy each other, like children in a line.

perspectives.who: Edmund Stoner, a British physicist, in the 1930s
perspectives.explanation: The electrons are not stuck to single atoms. They roam through the whole metal, like a crowd. The whole crowd can find it easier if more of them spin one way.
Both pictures are partly right. For iron, nickel and cobalt, the roaming picture fits better, but exact predictions are still hard.

explanations.art: Two pictures of a metal: on the left atoms in a grid, each holding a tiny arrow that its neighbours copy, on the right a crowd of electrons drifting through the grid, mostly pointing one way.
explanations.context: Scientists agree on which metals are magnetic. This card is about the deeper question of why, which has more than one answer.

explanations.concept: Everything answers a magnet a little
explanations.definition: Almost every material is pushed away, very weakly, by a magnet. This is called being diamagnetic. Some are pulled very weakly instead.
explanations.description: When we say wood, water or aluminium is non-magnetic, we really mean a fridge magnet cannot move it. A much stronger magnet can show a tiny reaction. In the 1990s, a physicist called Andre Geim floated a live frog in the air. He worked in the Netherlands and used a very strong magnet. The frog was not hurt. It just hovered, calmly. Frogs are mostly water, and water is pushed away from magnets a tiny bit. In a strong enough magnet, that tiny push can hold up the whole frog. Geim later won a Nobel Prize for a different material, graphene, a sheet of carbon one atom thick. So non-magnetic really means not pulled enough for us to notice.
examples: A very strong magnet can make a drop of water float in the air. A frog floats in an even stronger one.
Aluminium is pulled by a magnet extremely weakly. Copper, gold and silver are pushed away very weakly.
An MRI scanner in a hospital has a huge magnet. You lie inside it and feel no pull at all, unless you carry steel.
explanations.art: A small green frog floating in mid-air inside a tall cylinder magnet, looking very relaxed.
explanations.context: Is a non-magnetic thing really untouched by magnets? This card shows that even a frog reacts to a strong enough magnet.

explanations.definition: Every magnetic material stops being magnetic when it gets hot enough. The heat where this happens is called its Curie point.
explanations.description: Heat makes atoms jiggle. When iron is hot enough, the jiggling wins over the lining up, and the domains break apart. For iron, this happens at about 770 degrees Celsius, when it glows red. For nickel it is about 358 degrees. A French scientist, Pierre Curie, measured this carefully in 1895. Cool the iron again, and it becomes magnetic again. This is why you should never heat a magnet. It can also be why a magnet that is hit or dropped many times gets weaker. This is not safe to try at home, so we watch it in a video.
examples: A red-hot nail is not pulled by a magnet. When it cools it is pulled again.
A magnet left on a hot stove will lose strength.
Nickel loses its magnetism at about 358 degrees Celsius, iron at about 770 degrees.
explanations.art: Three panels: a cold nail clinging to a magnet, a red-hot nail falling away from it, and the cooled nail clinging again.
explanations.context: Can a magnetic thing stop being magnetic? This card explains what heat does.

explanations.concept: Magnets without metal: lodestone and ferrite
explanations.definition: Some magnetic materials are not metals. Lodestone is a rock. Ferrite is a ceramic, like a very hard pot. Both contain iron joined with oxygen.
explanations.description: Magnetite is a dark mineral made of iron joined with oxygen. A piece of it that is already a magnet is called a lodestone. People found lodestones thousands of years ago. In Sanskrit, the word for a magnet is ayaskanta, which means loved by iron. Today, many magnets on fridges are ferrite. Ferrite is a ceramic made by baking iron oxide, which is a bit like rust, with other powders. The thin bendy fridge magnet sheets are ferrite powder mixed into rubber. So a magnet can be made without any shiny metal. The rule that only metals are magnetic is a good one for kitchen objects, but not a law of nature. Ordinary brown rust is only very faintly pulled. A rusty nail still sticks, because there is iron under the rust.
examples: A black ceramic magnet from a loudspeaker is not metal.
A bendy fridge magnet sheet is powder mixed into rubber.
Black sand on some beaches contains magnetite grains, and a magnet picks them out.
explanations.art: A dark lodestone rock, a ceramic loudspeaker magnet and a bendy fridge magnet sheet in a row, each lifting a pin.
explanations.context: Are all magnetic materials metals? This card shows some that are not.

explanations.description: A lodestone is a rock that is already a magnet, with no one having touched it. Most pieces of magnetite are not magnets. So what turned a few into magnets? Scientists have more than one idea, and they do not agree yet.
examples: Lodestones are rare. Most magnetite rocks do not pull iron at all.
Many lodestones have been found near places where lightning has struck.

perspectives.who: Peter Wasilewski and Gunther Kletetschka, American scientists, in 1999
perspectives.explanation: Lightning did it. A lightning bolt carries a huge electric current, which makes a very strong magnetic field for a moment. That could magnetise the rock it strikes.

Slow cooling might do it. When hot rock cools deep underground, it can lock in a weak magnetic direction from the Earth's own magnetic field. That could explain weakly magnetic rocks, but not the very strong lodestones.

explanations.art: A lightning bolt hitting a dark rock on a hillside, and iron pins afterwards clinging to the rock.
explanations.context: The first magnets people found were rocks. This card asks how a rock ever became a magnet.

explanations.concept: The pull goes through things, and weakens with distance
explanations.definition: A magnet's pull goes through paper, cloth, plastic, wood, glass and water almost as if they were not there. But the pull gets weaker quickly as the gap gets bigger.
explanations.description: Put a paper clip on a table, and hold a magnet above a sheet of paper over it. The clip still jumps up. Add more sheets, and at some point the clip stops jumping. The paper did not block the pull. The thicker stack just put the magnet too far away. A stronger magnet can reach through more sheets. Non-magnetic materials let the pull pass through. But a magnetic material is different. A steel plate that sticks to the magnet grabs the pull for itself. Steel that does not stick lets the pull pass, like paper.
examples: A fridge magnet can hold a drawing, since the pull goes through paper to the steel door.
A magnet under a table can drag a clip across the top.
A strong magnet can drag a clip through the side of a glass of water.
explanations.art: A magnet beneath a table dragging a paper clip on top, next to a glass of water with a clip being pulled up the side.
explanations.context: Does anything block a magnet? This card explains the results of the Through the Paper experiment.

explanations.concept: The Earth has an iron heart
explanations.definition: The centre of the Earth is mostly iron, with some nickel. The outer part of the core is liquid, and its flowing makes the Earth's magnetic field.
explanations.description: Deep below your feet, past the rock, lies a ball of iron and nickel. It is about as wide as the planet Mars. The outer part is liquid, and the inner part is solid, squeezed hard. In 1936 a Danish scientist called Inge Lehmann studied earthquake waves. She worked out that there is a solid ball inside the liquid. She kept her measurements on index cards in boxes. The core is far too hot to be a permanent magnet, since it is much hotter than iron's Curie point. Instead, scientists think its liquid iron flows and swirls, and that swirling makes the magnetic field which a compass feels. Iron also falls from space as meteorites. A magnet can even pull tiny bits of space dust off a rooftop.
examples: The Earth's field makes a compass needle point north.
Iron meteorites are mostly iron and nickel. A magnet picks them up.
Tiny space dust grains, called micrometeorites, can be found on roofs with a magnet.
explanations.art: A cut-open Earth showing a solid inner ball, a swirling liquid outer layer, the rocky mantle and the crust, with faint curved lines leaving the Earth.
explanations.context: Why does a compass work? This card links the iron in your almirah to the iron at the centre of the Earth.

explanations.definition: Scientists think most of the iron in the universe was made inside stars, and scattered into space when stars exploded.
explanations.description: The early universe had almost only hydrogen and helium. Stars made heavier atoms inside them by squeezing lighter ones together. A big star can build atoms up to iron and nickel at its centre. After that, squeezing does not give out energy, and the star collapses and explodes. Some small, dead stars in pairs can blow up in another way. They make a lot of iron too. The iron flew into space, and became part of new stars, planets and, eventually, almirahs. So the iron nail in your hand contains atoms made in a star that died before our Sun was born. The iron in your blood has the same story.
examples: Iron meteorites carry iron that formed inside an old planet's core.
The iron in your blood, in haemoglobin, was also made in stars.
explanations.art: A bright star exploding with iron-coloured sparks flying outward, one spark landing on a young planet and another in a child's hand as a nail.
explanations.context: Where did iron come from? This card follows the nail in your hand back to a star.

explanations.concept: Living magnets: bacteria, and a debate about birds
explanations.description: Some living things carry magnets inside them. Magnetotactic bacteria make tiny chains of magnetite crystals, like a string of beads. The chain acts as a compass needle. A scientist called Richard Blakemore described them in 1975. Some historians say an Italian scientist, Salvatore Bellini, saw them in 1963, but few people read his work. Many animals can also sense the Earth's magnetic field. Scientists have shown this in birds, turtles and fish. But how they do it is a puzzle, and scientists have more than one idea.
examples: Magnetotactic bacteria swim along the Earth's magnetic field lines.
Migrating birds seem to use the magnetic field, along with the stars and the Sun.

perspectives.who: Joseph Kirschvink, a scientist in America, and others
perspectives.explanation: Animals may have tiny magnetite crystals in their bodies that turn like compass needles.

perspectives.who: Thorsten Ritz, Klaus Schulten and others, in 2000
perspectives.explanation: A light-sensitive protein in the eye, called cryptochrome, may let birds see the field, using quantum effects in its electrons.
Birds may use both ideas, one for direction and one for position. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A string of tiny dark crystals inside a bacterium pointing along arrows, and a small migrating bird above a landscape with faint curved field lines.
explanations.context: Do any living things use magnetic materials? This card shows two real stories, one settled and one still argued about.

explanations.concept: Super-strong magnets and why they are dangerous
explanations.definition: The strongest everyday magnets are made from a mixture of the metals neodymium, iron and boron. They can pinch skin, and they can badly hurt a child who swallows two.
explanations.description: In 1982, two scientists found a new kind of magnet. They worked separately. Masato Sagawa worked in Japan, and John Croat in the United States. They mixed neodymium, iron and boron, and made a magnet far stronger than any before. These magnets are inside headphones, phones, electric cars and wind turbines. Neodymium is a rare earth, a group of metals that is hard to dig up and to clean. These magnets are so strong that two swallowed apart can snap together through the gut wall. That needs an operation. That is why this unit uses only ordinary fridge magnets. If you find tiny shiny round magnets, keep them from little children.
examples: Neodymium magnets are in earphones and the motors of electric cars.
A tiny neodymium magnet can lift a heavy steel tool. A fridge magnet cannot.
explanations.art: A tiny silver disc magnet lifting a heavy steel spanner, with a big red cross next to a child's mouth.
explanations.context: Are some magnets much stronger than a fridge magnet? This card is about the strongest ones, and a safety rule.

agreed.text: A magnet pulls iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt.
agreed.evidence: People have tested this for thousands of years. Children repeat it in classrooms every day with nails, pins and paper clips.

agreed.text: Not every metal is magnetic. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are not.
agreed.evidence: Foil, copper wire, brass diyas and gold rings are ignored by a fridge magnet. Scrap dealers use this every day to separate iron from other metals.

agreed.text: Magnetism comes from electrons, which spin like tiny magnets.
agreed.evidence: In 1915, Albert Einstein and Wander de Haas hung an iron rod and flipped its magnetism. The rod twisted a little, which showed that magnetism comes from the spin of electrons.

agreed.text: In iron, nickel and cobalt, the tiny magnets line up in patches called domains.
agreed.evidence: Pierre-Ernest Weiss proposed domains in 1907. In 1931, Francis Bitter used a fine magnetic powder to show the patches on a polished metal surface.

agreed.text: Heat destroys magnetism. Every magnetic material has a heat, its Curie point, above which it is not magnetic.
agreed.evidence: Pierre Curie measured it in 1895. The Curie point of iron is about 770 degrees Celsius.

agreed.text: A magnet test can show that a thing contains iron, nickel or cobalt. It cannot show that a thing is a particular metal.
agreed.evidence: A thing that sticks must contain a magnetic material. But brass, aluminium, copper, gold, silver and some steels all fail to stick, so not sticking tells us little.

challenging.who: Many children and grown-ups, and some old books
challenging.for: Magnets and metals seem to go together. The magnets we use stick to the metal door of a fridge, and a metal nail.
challenging.against: Aluminium foil, copper wire, brass diyas, gold and silver are all ignored by a fridge magnet. Out of about ninety kinds of natural element, only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic at room temperature.
challenging.context: This card is about the most common mistake about magnets, and how a single test can fix it.

challenging.for: Many steel tumblers, katoris and thalis really do not stick to a magnet.
challenging.against: Only the nickel-rich kinds of stainless steel are non-magnetic. Others, which have chromium but little nickel, stick well. Induction stove pans are made from those. Even the non-sticking kind can become a little magnetic where it has been bent.
challenging.context: Many people say that stainless steel does not stick to magnets. This card checks that claim.

challenging.claim: A magnet can tell you whether a coin or a ring is real gold or silver.
challenging.for: Gold and silver are not magnetic. If something sticks, it contains iron or a similar metal, so it is not pure gold.
challenging.against: Many fake metals also do not stick, such as brass, copper or aluminium. A magnet test can catch some fakes, but it cannot prove that anything is real. Other tests are needed.
challenging.context: Can a magnet find fake gold? This card shows what the test can and cannot tell us.

challenging.claim: The iron in your blood makes your body magnetic.
challenging.who: A popular joke and some websites
challenging.for: Blood contains iron, and iron is magnetic.
challenging.against: Your whole body holds only about as much iron as a small nail. It is locked inside molecules, such as haemoglobin, and is not lined up in domains. You are not pulled by a magnet. Hospitals put people inside huge magnets for MRI scans, and nothing pulls them, unless they carry steel.
challenging.context: Blood has iron in it, and iron is magnetic. So are we magnetic? This card checks.

challenging.claim: The Earth is a giant bar magnet, with a big permanent magnet inside.
challenging.for: A compass needle behaves as if there were a giant bar magnet inside the Earth.
challenging.against: The Earth's core is much hotter than iron's Curie point, so it cannot hold a permanent magnet. Scientists think the field comes from flowing liquid iron. This also explains why the field has flipped direction many times in the Earth's history.
challenging.context: A common picture of the Earth is a bar magnet inside. This card checks that picture.

challenging.claim: A magnet's pull shows that it is alive.
challenging.who: Thales of Miletus, a Greek thinker, about 2,600 years ago, as reported by Aristotle
challenging.for: A lodestone moves iron without anyone pushing it, which is what living things do.
challenging.against: We now know the pull comes from electrons lined up inside the rock, not from a soul. But Thales was one of the first to look for a cause inside nature, instead of blaming a god. That was a big step.
challenging.context: This card is about one of the oldest ideas about magnets, and why it was still a good question.

challenging.claim: Garlic makes a magnet lose its power.
challenging.who: Sailors and writers in old times, believed for centuries
challenging.for: Many people repeated it, and it was in respected books.
challenging.against: William Gilbert, an English doctor, wrote a whole book on magnets in 1600, called De Magnete. He tested the garlic claim and found it was false. He said you should trust experiments over old books.
challenging.context: For hundreds of years, many people believed garlic could spoil a magnet. This card is about how William Gilbert checked.

challenging.claim: Birds find their way using tiny iron compasses in their beaks.
challenging.who: Some scientists, and many science books
challenging.for: Iron-rich cells were found in the beaks of some birds, and iron can sense a magnetic field.
challenging.against: Later work found that many of those iron-rich cells were white blood cells, which are not sensors at all. Other experiments point to a light-sensitive protein in the eye. Scientists still do not agree.
challenging.context: How do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field? This card shows a popular answer that was questioned.

big_questions.q: Out of about ninety natural elements, only three are magnetic in a room. Why do you think the universe made so few?
big_questions.hint: In most atoms, the tiny magnets cancel out in pairs. What would the world be like if every metal were magnetic?

big_questions.q: If a wooden spoon has countless tiny magnets inside it, why is it not magnetic?
big_questions.hint: Think of a crowd where everyone points a different way, and a crowd where everyone points the same way. Which crowd would you notice?

big_questions.q: A magnet pulls a nail across a gap with nothing touching it. What is in the gap?
big_questions.hint: Scientists say a magnetic field fills the gap. A field is something that can push or pull things in the space around a magnet. Is a field a thing, or only an idea?

big_questions.q: A frog floated in a magnet, and frogs are not magnetic. So is anything truly non-magnetic?
big_questions.hint: Maybe 'non-magnetic' is a word for 'too weak for me to notice'. What other words in science work that way?

big_questions.q: The iron in your almirah was made in a star that exploded before the Sun was born. What does that make you and the almirah?
big_questions.hint: Where did the iron in your own blood come from?

big_questions.q: A magnet test can say 'no, this is not gold', but it cannot say 'yes, this is gold'. What other tests in life can only say no?
big_questions.hint: Think about a smoke alarm, a fever, or a doctor's check. When can a no be trusted more than a yes?

big_questions.q: The Earth's magnetic field comes from flowing iron deep below. Would life be different without it?
big_questions.hint: The field helps push away fast particles from the Sun. Scientists argue about how much it matters for life. Mars has almost no field. Venus has none either.

big_questions.q: Thales thought a lodestone must be alive because it moved iron. Is there something else that moves without being touched that you feel is alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Moon moving the sea, or a plant turning to the Sun. Which things are alive, and how can we tell?

big_questions.q: Waste pickers and kabadiwalas sort metal by hand every day, work that magnets and machines do in rich countries. Who should be paid for sorting the world's rubbish?
big_questions.hint: Who uses the metal they sort? Who is paid, and how much?

big_questions.q: Much of India's iron ore is dug from hills in Odisha and Jharkhand. Adivasi communities have lived there for generations. Who should decide whether a hill is dug up?
big_questions.hint: Who gains from the iron? Who loses the forest? Is there a fair way to share?

big_questions.q: Inge Lehmann found the Earth's solid inner core with a shoebox of cards, working almost alone. Why do you think great ideas sometimes come from quiet people with simple tools?
big_questions.hint: Think of Salvatore Bellini, who saw magnetic bacteria in 1963 when few people read his paper. Who else gets forgotten?

big_questions.q: In a wooden spoon, the tiny magnets cancel out to nothing. Is 'nothing' always empty?
big_questions.hint: A crowd where everyone pushes a different way can be perfectly still. Is it empty, or perfectly balanced?

big_questions.q: Heusler mixed three non-magnetic metals and made a magnet. Can a team of ordinary people become more than the sum of their parts?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cricket team, a family or a village. What do they do together that none can do alone?

story.title: What the Magnet Said No To
story.note: Moradabad in Uttar Pradesh really is called the Brass City, and brass plated onto steel is real. Zainab, her grandfather and the trader are made up.
text: Zainab's grandfather could no longer see the colour of metal. A cloud had grown over both his eyes, like milk in tea. But he could still hear it.

Every morning, in the workshop in Moradabad, the city of brass, he held up a new sheet of metal. Then he flicked it with his fingernail. If the note came back long and warm, he nodded. If it came back short and dull, he frowned. 'Brass sings,' he would say. 'Everything else only talks.'

Zainab was ten, and she swept the floor. It was a big floor, covered in filings and sawdust and tiny bits of wire, and the worst part was the pins. The workers used pins and tacks and little nails to hold their patterns, and the pins fell everywhere. So Zainab had tied a small flat magnet to a string at her waist. She dragged it across the floor like a fishing line, and the pins leapt up and clung to it. At the end of each day she wiped them off into a tin. She called the magnet Chhoti Machhli, the little fish.

That week the workshop had a huge order. A shop in Delhi wanted two hundred brass lamp stands for Diwali. The sheets of brass would come on a truck on Monday morning. Her grandfather had been waiting for the order for three months, because money was short.

The truck came. The trader was a man in a clean white kurta with a gold ring on every other finger. His workers carried in the sheets, and they were beautiful. They were the colour of a ripe mango. Her grandfather held out his hand, and the trader put a sheet in it.

He flicked it. The note came back. It was short, but the workshop was loud with the truck, so who could be sure? He weighed it in his hand. He ran his thumb along the edge. 'Good,' he said at last, though he sounded like a man trying to convince himself. 'It will do.'

Zainab was standing by the door with her broom. Something bothered her, and she could not say what. So she did the only thing she knew how to do. She unwound Chhoti Machhli from her waist, and let it dangle over the top sheet in the pile.
The little magnet swung once, and then it jumped. It snapped onto the sheet with a click that everyone in the room could hear.

Nobody spoke. Zainab pulled the magnet off with both hands, because it was stuck quite hard, and held it over the next sheet. Click. And the next. Click. She went down the pile. It stuck to every one of them.
'That is a toy,' said the trader quickly. 'A child's toy. It means nothing.'

Her grandfather had gone very still. 'Zainab,' he said, 'go to the shelf. Bring me the old diya, the one my father made.' She ran. The diya was brass, black with age, and as heavy as a fist. She put it in his hands, and then she held Chhoti Machhli close.
It swung once, and it did not jump. It did not even twitch. It hung from its string, over the old lamp, and just turned slowly.

'Brass is copper and zinc,' her grandfather said, to nobody in particular. 'Neither of them cares for a magnet. But iron cares. Steel cares very much.' He turned his clouded eyes towards the trader. 'Underneath your lovely mango colour, there is steel, isn't there? A thin coat of brass on top, like a coat of butter on a roti.'
The trader said many things, some loud and some soft. But in the end he picked up his sheets and went back to his truck, because it is hard to argue with something that clicks.
That night, as the lamps in the lane were being lit, Zainab sat with her grandfather on the step. 'Dada,' she said. 'If the magnet had not stuck, would that have meant the sheets were real brass?'

He was quiet for a long time. A moth went round the lamp. 'No,' he said at last. 'It could have been aluminium with yellow paint on it. It could have been something I have never heard of. Your fish can only tell me what a thing is not. It cannot tell me what it is.' He smiled. 'But today I needed to hear a no more than I needed to hear a yes. A good test, Zainab, is a small honest voice. It says one true thing.'
The next morning he did not flick any sheets. He held out his hand, palm up, and said, 'Teach me to use the fish.'

So she taught him. She guided his fingers until he could feel the little tug of the string, or the lack of it. The new sheets, the real ones, came a week later from a different trader. One by one they went under the magnet in his old hands. Each time, the little fish hung there, calm and still, and did not stick at all.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a magnet pulls iron and steel, but not brass, which is made of copper and zinc. So when a magnet sticks to a sheet that is meant to be brass, the sheet must have steel underneath. The magnet cannot tell you what a thing is, only that it contains iron, nickel or cobalt. Zainab's grandfather also teaches a lesson about tests. When the magnet sticks, it gives a clear no to the question 'is this solid brass?' When it does not stick, it gives only a maybe. The story also asks who is trusted to know. The expert's ears failed him in a noisy room. The child who swept the floor, with a simple tool, saw what he could not.
ask: Why did the magnet stick to the sheets but not to the old diya?
What was underneath the thin layer of brass on the sheets?
Zainab's grandfather said a magnet could tell him what a thing is not, but not what it is. What do you think he meant?
Why did the trader call the magnet a toy? Why did it still matter?
Who in your home or school notices small things that others miss?

games.title: Stick or Skip?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 32 object cards to cut out (the star cards are the tricky ones)
items: STAR: A pan for an induction stove
STAR: The bottom of a steel pressure cooker

rules: Cut out the 32 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down. Put the two mats on the table.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: will a magnet stick to it or skip it? Put the card on the STICK mat or the SKIP mat, and say one reason. A good reason wins one star.
If you have a magnet, test it. A correct guess wins one more star.
If you draw a STAR card, you may say 'test it' instead of guessing. If you do, and the object is on a STAR card, you win two stars. Guess wrong on a STAR card, and you lose one star.
When the cards run out, the player with the most stars wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mats on the table, STICK on one side and SKIP on the other. 2. Shuffle the 32 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the star tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: A magnet is choosy. Every card shows a thing from our homes. For each one, we decide. Will a magnet stick to it, or skip it?
flow.kid: Put out the two mats, STICK and SKIP. Mix the cards and put them face down. For each card, decide if the magnet will stick or skip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stick or Skip?. It is a card game about which everyday things a magnet pulls. Here you set it up.

flow.do: Play a practice round with the card 'Iron nail'.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'Iron nail.' Will a magnet stick to it or skip it?
flow.kid: Practice card: iron nail. Stick or skip? Tap your answer.

good: A nail is made of iron.
Iron is magnetic.

check.q: Iron nail. What will a magnet do?
check.why: A nail is made of iron, and a magnet pulls iron. Picking skip usually means thinking that a small thing is too light to feel a magnet. But a nail jumps to a magnet easily.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out, places it on a mat and gives a reason. 2. Test it with a real magnet if you can. 3. Give stars for good reasons and correct guesses.
flow.say: When you place your card, tell me why. A good reason names what the thing is made of.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card and put it on STICK or SKIP. Say why, and test it if you can. Each good reason wins a star.
flow.parent: Good reasons for STICK: the object is iron or steel. For SKIP: it is plastic, wood, glass, cloth, stone, or a metal like aluminium, copper, brass, gold or silver. The pencil lead is graphite, which is a form of carbon, and it is not pulled.

ask.q: A one-rupee coin is a STAR card. Why is it tricky?
good: Some coins are made of a steel that sticks, and some are made of other metals.
It depends on the coin.

flow.do: When a STAR card comes up, stop and talk. Ask your child whether they would like to guess or say 'test it'.
flow.say: A STAR card! Do you want to guess, or say 'test it'? Guessing wrong costs a star. Testing wins two.
flow.kid: A STAR card! Guess, or say 'test it'? A wrong guess costs a star.
flow.think: Why is saying 'test it' sometimes the cleverest move in science?

check.q: Steel tumbler. What is the smartest answer?
options: Test it, because some steels stick and some do not
check.why: The tumbler is steel, but steel is a mixture and the mixture decides. Many tumblers are the nickel-rich kind and do not stick. Others do. So the best answer is to test it. Picking stick or skip each only works for some tumblers. Scientists test when the answer depends.

flow.do: Count the stars to find the winner. Then look at the two piles. Ask which pile is bigger.
flow.say: Count your stars. Who won? Now look at the two piles. Which pile is bigger? Is it mostly iron and steel in the STICK pile?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Who won? Which pile is bigger, STICK or SKIP?
flow.think: Why do you think most things on the SKIP pile are so different from each other?

games.context: This is a card game about which everyday things a magnet sticks to and which it skips. The tricky STAR cards teach that you must sometimes test.

games.title: The Magnet Court
games.players: 2 to 5 players: one judge and the others as lawyers, taking turns

printables.title: 13 case cards to cut out
items: Rani says: The spoon stuck to the magnet. So the spoon has iron in it.
Imran says: The key did not stick. So it is made of brass.
Asha says: The tumbler did not stick. So it is not made of steel.
Dev says: The coin did not stick. So it is real silver.
Meena says: The foil ball did not stick. So my magnet must be broken.
Zoya says: The nail stuck. So all metals stick.
Kabir says: The pin stuck. So the pin is not made of gold.
Lata says: The magnet stuck to my tin can. So the can is made of tin.
Ravi says: The toy car stuck to the magnet. So the whole car is made of iron.
Sana says: The bottom of my steel pot stuck. So the bottom has a magnetic metal in it.
Joseph says: The magnet pulled a clip through a plate. So the plate is magnetic.
Nisha says: My ring did not stick. So it is pure gold.
Tara says: A frog floated in a very strong magnet. So a frog is magnetic like iron.

printables.title: Three verdict paddles
items: NOT PROVED: it might be true, but the evidence does not show it
WRONG: the evidence shows it is false, or the reasoning is faulty

rules: Shuffle the 13 case cards and put them face down.
One player is the judge. The judge reads a case out loud.
Everyone else raises a verdict paddle: PROVED, NOT PROVED or WRONG. They say why in one sentence.
The judge says what they think, and talks it over with the lawyers. A correct verdict with a good reason wins two points. A correct verdict alone wins one.
Swap the judge after each case. After six cases, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Make the three paddles from paper. 2. Shuffle the case cards. 3. Choose a judge.
flow.say: A magnet test gives us evidence. But does the evidence prove what people say it proves? Today we are a court. We decide each case.
flow.kid: Make three paddles: PROVED, NOT PROVED, WRONG. Pick a judge. Mix the cases. We will test what people claim.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Magnet Court. In this game, you decide whether a claim about a magnet test is proved, not proved, or wrong.

flow.do: Read the practice case: 'Rani says: the spoon stuck to the magnet. So the spoon has iron in it.' Let everyone raise a paddle.
flow.say: Practice case. Rani says the spoon stuck, so it has iron in it. What is your verdict?
flow.kid: Practice case. Rani says the spoon stuck, so it has iron in it. Proved, not proved, or wrong?

good: Only iron, nickel, cobalt or things containing them stick.
A thing that sticks must have a magnetic material in it.

check.q: The spoon stuck to the magnet. What is Rani's claim that the spoon has iron in it?
check.why: In an ordinary kitchen, only iron, nickel, cobalt and their mixtures stick to a magnet. Iron is by far the most common. So Rani can say the spoon contains a magnetic metal, nearly always iron. Picking not proved usually means thinking a magnet can be fooled. It can only be fooled by something that is itself magnetic, so it still tells us about iron or nickel.

flow.do: Play the cases one by one. Let each lawyer give a reason before the judge decides. Write each verdict on the court record.
flow.say: Take a case. Read it. Raise your paddle. Say why in one sentence. Then the judge decides.
flow.kid: Take turns as judge. Read a case. Everyone raises a paddle and says why. The judge decides.
flow.parent: Verdicts: Rani PROVED. Imran NOT PROVED, because aluminium and copper do not stick either. Asha WRONG, because some steels do not stick. Dev NOT PROVED, because brass and aluminium do not stick either. Meena WRONG, because the foil is not magnetic. Test the magnet on a nail. Zoya WRONG. Kabir PROVED. Lata WRONG, because tin is not magnetic. The can is steel with a thin coat of tin. Ravi NOT PROVED, because it may be plastic with a steel axle. Sana PROVED for the bottom. Joseph WRONG, because the pull goes through non-magnetic plates. Nisha NOT PROVED. Tara WRONG, because a frog is only very weakly pushed away.

ask.q: Why is Imran's case not proved?
good: Brass does not stick, but aluminium and copper do not stick either.
A no from a magnet cannot tell us what a thing is.

flow.do: Look at the court record. Count which verdict came up most often. Ask which case was hardest.
flow.say: Which verdict came up most often? Which case was hardest? What does that tell us about magnet tests?
flow.kid: Which verdict came up most? Which case was hardest? What did you learn about magnet tests?

check.q: A magnet test is best at which of these jobs?
options: Showing that a thing is not made only of non-magnetic stuff
check.why: If a thing sticks, it must contain a magnetic material. That is a solid yes about iron, nickel or cobalt. If it does not stick, it could be brass, aluminium, copper, gold, silver, or a steel of the non-sticking kind. A no tells us much less. Picking the other two usually means expecting a magnet to name a metal. A magnet only separates magnetic from non-magnetic.

flow.think: Which other tests in life can say 'no' clearly but cannot say 'yes'?

games.context: This is a game where you act as a judge in a court. For each case, you decide whether a person's claim about a magnet test is proved, not proved, or wrong.

items.p: Which of these does a magnet pull?
items.why: A nail is made of iron, and a magnet pulls iron. Picking wood, glass or plastic usually means thinking that any small light thing will be pulled. But a magnet ignores all of these.

items.p: A magnet pulls every metal.
items.why: False. A magnet pulls iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. It ignores aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver. Believing it pulls all metals is the most common mistake about magnets.

items.p: Sort these things. Does a magnet pull them or not?
items.why: The nail, clip, pin and almirah contain iron. Foil, brass, copper and wood do not respond to a magnet. Brass and copper are shiny metals, but shine does not matter.

items.p: A material that a magnet pulls is called ____.
items.why: Magnetic means a magnet pulls it. Be careful: it does not mean that the thing is itself a magnet.

items.p: Which of these metals is NOT pulled by a magnet?
items.why: Aluminium is not magnetic. Iron, nickel and cobalt are. Picking nickel or cobalt usually means thinking that unusual metals are non-magnetic. But those two are magnetic, like iron.

items.p: Match each alloy to what it is made from.
items.why: An alloy is a metal mixed with something else. The mixture often behaves very differently from its ingredients.

items.p: Look at the table from a magnet test. Which group had the most things that stuck?
items.why: The table shows 5 iron or steel things stuck, and nothing from the other groups. Picking other metals usually means thinking that all metals behave the same way.
items.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 objects with a magnet and group the results. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

items.p: A steel spoon sticks to a magnet, but a steel tumbler does not. Why?
opts: Steel is a mixture, and the tumbler's mixture has things in it, like nickel, that stop the pull
The tumbler is not made of metal
items.why: Steel is an alloy, and different steels have different mixtures. Nickel-rich steel is not pulled much. Picking 'not made of metal' usually means thinking all metal things behave the same. A tumbler is metal. It is just a different kind of steel.

items.p: A magnet must touch a paper clip to pull it.
items.why: False. The magnet's pull works across a gap. A clip jumps up to a magnet before they touch.

items.p: A fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge door. What does the paper do?
opts: It lets the pull go through to the steel door
items.why: Paper is non-magnetic, so the pull goes straight through. The steel door does the sticking. Picking 'paper is magnetic' usually means thinking that the magnet is holding the paper. The magnet and the door are holding each other, with the paper in between.

items.p: Put the steps of a magnet test in the right order.
items: Hold the magnet on each object for three seconds
Write the result in the table
items.why: We guess first, so we know when we are surprised. Then we test the same way each time, record, and look for a pattern.

items.p: Brass is copper mixed with ____.
items.why: Brass is made of copper and zinc. Neither is magnetic, so brass is not either.

items.p: Rohan says: 'The key is shiny, so the magnet will stick to it.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. Shiny things are not always magnetic. A brass key is shiny, but a magnet does not stick to brass. A magnet sticks to iron and steel, whether they are shiny or not.
items.why: Shine tells us how light bounces off a surface. It tells us nothing about whether a magnet will pull it.

items.p: A magnet did not stick to a ring. What can we be sure of?
opts: The ring has no magnetic metal in a form this magnet can feel
items.why: If a ring does not stick, it is not pulled. But gold, silver, brass and aluminium rings all fail to stick, so we cannot tell which it is. Picking 'gold' usually means expecting a magnet to name the metal. It can only say what a thing is not.

items.p: Draw a magnet, a paper clip and a gap between them. Draw what happens to the clip.
items.a: The clip is drawn leaping up across the gap to the magnet. A small arrow points from the clip to the magnet.
items.why: The magnet pulls the clip across a gap without touching it.
items.art: A blank page with a bar magnet on top and a paper clip on a table below.

items.p: How does a scrap dealer use a magnet?
opts: To pull iron and steel out of a mixed heap
items.why: A magnet lifts iron and steel and leaves other metals like aluminium, copper and brass behind. Picking 'gold from silver' usually means expecting a magnet to tell metals apart. It cannot, because neither is magnetic.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which object picked up the most clips?
items.why: The tallest bar is the iron nail, with 6 clips. Picking copper wire usually means misreading a bar of 0 as the most. A bar of 0 means the wire picked up nothing.
items.context: In the lending experiment, a magnet lends its pull to a nail. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: clips each object picked up while touching the magnet

items.p: A magnet's pull is blocked completely by one sheet of paper.
items.why: False. A magnet pulls a clip right through a sheet of paper. It takes a very thick stack to stop the pull. That is because of the distance, not because the paper blocks it.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which magnet is the strongest?
items.why: The bar magnet reached through 30 sheets, the most. A stronger magnet reaches through more paper. Picking the small fridge magnet usually means thinking the smallest number is the best, as in a race.
items.context: In the Through the Paper experiment, you count how many sheets of paper a magnet can reach through. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: sheets of paper the pull reached through

items.p: A tiny patch inside iron where many atoms point their tiny magnets the same way is called a ____.
items.why: A domain is a patch with billions of atoms lined up. A nail is full of domains, pointing in different directions.

items.p: A wooden spoon is full of tiny magnets, but it is not magnetic. Why?
opts: Its tiny magnets point every which way and cancel out
A wooden spoon is too light
items.why: In wood, the tiny magnets point in all directions, so the pulls cancel. In iron, neighbours line up in groups. Picking 'wood has no atoms' usually means thinking only metals are made of atoms. Everything is.

items.p: When you pull a nail away from a magnet, it slowly loses its pull.
items.why: True. The magnet had lined up the nail's tiny magnets. Without the magnet, most of them drift out of line, and the pull fades.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: showed that heat makes magnets stop working
tested old beliefs about magnets, such as garlic
found the Earth's solid inner core
floated a frog in a very strong magnet
items.why: Each of them asked a question and tested it. Lehmann worked with earthquake waves, Curie with heat, Gilbert with careful experiments in 1600, and Geim with a huge magnet.

items.p: Why must a pan for an induction stove stick to a magnet?
opts: The stove works through magnetism, so the pan must be magnetic
So that it does not slide
items.why: An induction stove makes a changing magnetic field, which works well in a pan that a magnet sticks to. An aluminium pan or a nickel-rich steel pan often does not work. Picking 'does not slide' usually means thinking a magnet works like glue on the stove.

items.p: A trader gives you a gold-coloured sheet. The magnet sticks to it. What can you say about it? What can you not say?
items.a: I can say it has iron, nickel or cobalt inside, so it is not pure brass. I cannot say what it is made of. It might be steel with a thin gold-coloured coat.
items.why: A magnet sticking is a strong clue about what is inside. It does not name the whole material.

items.p: Will a magnet stick? Sort these.
items.why: Iron always sticks, and aluminium and wood never do. Steel tumblers, katoris and coins depend on exactly which mixture they are made from, so we test them.

items.p: A clip jumps up through 1 sheet of paper, but not through 40 sheets. Why?
opts: The magnet is now too far away to pull the clip
items.why: A magnet's pull gets weaker quickly with distance. Forty sheets only put the magnet farther away. Picking 'paper is magnetic' usually means thinking paper itself takes away the pull.

items.p: Put these in order of the heat at which they stop being magnetic, lowest first. Nickel stops at about 358 degrees Celsius, iron at about 770, and cobalt at about 1,115.
items.why: 358 is smaller than 770, which is smaller than 1,115. So nickel stops first, then iron, then cobalt.

items.p: Mixing metals that are not magnetic can never make a magnet.
items.why: False. In 1903, Fritz Heusler mixed copper, manganese and aluminium. None of them is magnetic, but the mixture was.

items.p: In the story, why did the magnet stick to the new sheets but not to the old diya?
items.a: The old diya was real brass, and brass is copper and zinc, so a magnet does not stick. The new sheets only had a thin coat of brass, with steel underneath, and a magnet sticks to steel.
items.why: The magnet answered a simple question about what was inside.

items.p: A steel fridge door and a wooden cupboard door stand side by side. A magnet sticks to only one. How can you make it stick to the wooden door?
opts: Fix a flat piece of steel onto the wood
items.why: The magnet sticks to steel. If a steel piece is fixed to the wood, the magnet has something to grip. Picking 'heat the magnet' usually means thinking that more energy means more pull. Heat actually weakens magnets.

items.p: Draw two squares. In one, draw the tiny magnets inside wood as arrows. In the other, draw the tiny magnets in a nail.
items.a: In the wood square, the arrows point in many different directions. In the nail square, the arrows are in patches, and all the arrows in each patch point the same way.
items.why: In wood, the arrows cancel. In iron, they line up in domains.
items.art: Two blank squares on a page.

items.p: A live frog floats in a very strong magnet. What does this show?
opts: Even non-magnetic things are pushed a tiny bit by a magnet
Frogs contain a lot of iron
items.why: Almost everything is pushed away very weakly by a magnet. A huge magnet can push hard enough to hold up a frog. Picking 'frogs contain a lot of iron' usually means thinking that floating needs a pull. Here it is a push, so iron is not the reason.

items.p: The Earth's core is mostly iron but is not a permanent magnet. Why not?
opts: It is much hotter than iron's Curie point
items.why: Iron stops being magnetic at about 770 degrees Celsius, and the core is far hotter. So the field must come from something else, which scientists think is flowing liquid iron. Picking 'too cold' gets the idea the wrong way round.

items.p: Explain why a copper wire is not pulled but an iron nail is. Use the words tiny magnets.
items.a: Every atom has electrons that act like tiny magnets. In iron, the tiny magnets line up in patches, so a magnet can turn the patches and pull the nail. In copper, the tiny magnets cancel each other out, so there is nothing for a magnet to pull.
items.why: The difference is not in the metals' colour or hardness. It is in how the tiny magnets inside behave.

items.p: Which statement about fridge magnets is true?
opts: Some magnets contain no shiny metal at all
All magnets are made only of iron
A ceramic can never be magnetic
items.why: Many fridge magnets are ferrite, a ceramic made of iron joined with oxygen. Picking 'a ceramic can never be magnetic' usually means thinking only shiny metal can be magnetic.

items.p: Most of the iron in an almirah was made inside a star.
items.why: True. Scientists think most iron was made inside big stars. It was blown out when they exploded, long before our Sun was born.

items.p: A magnet cannot tell a brass key from an aluminium key. Which test could?
opts: Feel how heavy each is, and look at its colour
items.why: Brass is heavier and yellower. Aluminium is lighter and silvery. A bigger magnet still ignores both. Heating them red-hot is dangerous and tells us little. Picking 'a bigger magnet' usually means thinking a stronger test will give a clearer answer. But the magnet is the wrong tool.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out which of two magnets is stronger. Say what you will keep the same.
items.a: I will use the same paper clip and the same paper. I will count how many sheets each magnet can reach through. I will start each magnet on top of the stack and try each twice. I change only the magnet.
items.why: A fair test changes just one thing and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: A ring sticks to a magnet. Tara says it cannot be pure silver. Is she right?
opts: Yes, silver is not magnetic, so something else is inside
Yes, but only if the ring is heavy
items.why: Silver is not magnetic. So a ring that sticks has a magnetic material in it, perhaps steel. This is the kind of thing a magnet can prove. Picking 'no, silver always sticks' mixes silver up with iron.

items.p: In 1963 Salvatore Bellini noticed bacteria that line up in a magnetic field, but his work was hardly read. In 1975 Richard Blakemore described them and became well known. What does this suggest?
opts: Credit does not always go to the first person who finds something
Only famous people can make discoveries
items.why: Historians now credit Bellini for noticing them first. Being first and being known are not the same. Picking 'Blakemore copied Bellini' goes further than the evidence. Blakemore found them independently.

items.p: Zainab's grandfather said, 'A good test is a small honest voice. It says one true thing.' What true thing did the magnet say? What could it not say?
items.a: The magnet said that the sheets had steel inside them, because they stuck. It could not say what the other metal was, or whether a sheet that did not stick was brass.
items.why: A test has limits. Knowing the limits is part of being a good scientist.

items.p: The bottom of a steel pan sticks to a magnet, but its sides do not. A sensible explanation is…
opts: The bottom has a magnetic steel disc added, so it works on an induction stove
items.why: Many pans have sides of nickel-rich steel and a magnetic disc fixed to the bottom. Picking 'the sides are plastic' usually means thinking a non-sticking surface must be a non-metal. But it is metal too.

items.p: If a magnet does not stick to a thing, the thing cannot be a metal.
items.why: False. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are metals, and a magnet does not stick to any of them.

items.p: Match each magnet material to where it is used.
items.why: Different magnets are good for different jobs. Ferrite is cheap and strong enough for a fridge door. Neodymium magnets are the strongest everyday kind.

items.p: Waste pickers and kabadiwalas sort metal by hand every day. Write two questions you would ask one of them, and one thing you would like to change.
items.a: For example: How do you know which metal is which? How much do you earn for a kilogram of iron? I would like to change how much they are paid, or give them gloves and safe tools.
items.why: Science is useful only when we also ask who does the work, and whether it is fair.

items.p: Which is the best evidence that the Earth's field comes from flowing liquid iron and not from a permanent magnet?
opts: The core is far hotter than iron's Curie point
items.why: Above its Curie point, iron cannot keep a permanent magnetism, so something else must be making the field. Picking 'compasses point north' is true, but it does not tell us how the field is made.

items.p: Draw the Earth cut in half. Label the solid inner core, the liquid outer core, the mantle and the crust.
items.a: A circle with four layers. In the middle, a small circle labelled solid inner core. Around it, a thick ring labelled liquid outer core. Then a thick ring of mantle, and a thin outer ring of crust.
items.why: Inge Lehmann found the solid inner core in 1936 from earthquake waves.

experiments.title: The Great Magnet Test: what does a magnet pick?
experiments.question: Which things does a magnet pull, and is there a pattern?
experiments.predict: Before you test anything, look at all 16 objects. Guess which ones the magnet will pull. Put your guesses in two piles, STICK and SKIP.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet every time. Hold it on each object for three seconds. Try each object twice, because one try can be a fluke. Change only the object.

materials.item: one fridge magnet or any ordinary magnet
an iron nail, a safety pin, a steel paper clip and a steel spoon
a steel katori or tumbler, and a coin
a ball of aluminium foil, a copper wire or copper lota, and a brass key or diya
a plastic spoon, a wooden pencil, a glass bangle, a piece of cotton cloth and a stone
two sheets of paper, one marked STICK and one marked SKIP
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the magnet away from phones, bank cards and watches. Never let a small child put a magnet in their mouth.

schedule.what: Guess. Test all 16 objects twice. Sort them. Find the pattern. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

flow.do: 1. Gather the 16 objects on a table. 2. Put out two sheets of paper, one marked STICK and one marked SKIP. 3. Ask your child to place each object on the sheet where they think it will go.
flow.say: Here are sixteen things from around our home. For each one, guess whether the magnet will pull it. Put it on STICK or SKIP.
flow.kid: Look at the 16 objects. For each one, guess. Will the magnet pull it? Put it on STICK or SKIP.

ask.q: Why did you put that one on STICK?
good: It is made of metal.
It is iron or steel.
It looks like a nail.
I think all metal sticks.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess yet. Fair testing has its own unit, Testing Materials. A guess that all metal sticks is the most common one, and it is the best thing to test. Write down which things go on each sheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Great Magnet Test. You will test 16 everyday things with a magnet, but first you guess.

flow.do: 1. Show how to test. Hold the magnet against one object for three seconds. 2. Lift the magnet slowly. 3. If the object lifts with the magnet, or the magnet clings, that is a stick. 4. Test the nail first, as a practice.
flow.say: Hold the magnet on the object and count to three. If it clings, or the object lifts with it, that is a stick. Let's try the nail first.
flow.kid: Hold the magnet on the object. Count to three. Does it cling? Try the iron nail first.
flow.parent: A weak fridge magnet may only cling to a flat object, and not lift it. That still counts as a stick. A thin steel spoon may cling weakly. That is a stick too.

check.q: Why do we hold the magnet on each object for three seconds, and test each one twice?
options: So that the test is fair, and one odd try cannot fool us
Because magnets only work after three seconds
check.why: A fair test treats every object the same way. Counting three seconds each time, and trying twice, stops one slip or fluke from giving the wrong answer. Picking 'magnets only work after three seconds' usually means thinking a magnet needs time to charge up. A magnet pulls at once, but our fingers can be clumsy.

flow.do: 1. Test the objects one at a time, twice each. 2. After each one, say it out loud, 'it stuck' or 'it did not stick'. 3. Write the result in the table. 4. Move the object onto the right sheet.
flow.say: Test them one by one. Say what happens each time. Then we'll write it in the table.
flow.kid: Test each object, twice. Say what happens out loud. Write it in your table.

good: The brass key did not stick.
The foil did not stick.
The steel tumbler did not stick.
The spoon stuck, but the tumbler did not.

flow.parent: Expect: the nail, pin and paper clip stick. The aluminium foil, copper, brass key, plastic, wood, glass, cloth and stone do not. The steel spoon and katori can vary. Many tumblers do not stick, and that is a real result, not a mistake. Coins vary too, so write down what you find.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Look at the two piles. Compare them with your guesses at the start. Count how many guesses were right.
flow.say: Look at your guesses. How many were right? Which ones were wrong, and what do you think now?
flow.kid: Look at your guesses. How many were right? Which ones were wrong?

good: No.
The foil, the key and the copper did not.
Only some of the metal things stuck.

flow.think: Is it the shine that makes a thing stick? Look at the brass key and the nail. Shine is one property of a material, and the unit Properties of Materials looks at many more.

flow.do: Look at the STICK pile. Ask what is the same about everything in it. Then look at the SKIP pile and ask what is the same about it.
flow.say: Look at everything in the STICK pile. What do they have in common? Now look at the SKIP pile.
flow.kid: Look at the STICK pile. What is the same? Now look at the SKIP pile.

check.q: In a typical test, everything that stuck to the magnet was…
check.why: The nail, pin, paper clip and steel spoon all contain iron. A shiny brass key and a shiny foil ball did not stick, so shiny is not the secret. Picking 'any metal' usually means thinking all metals are the same. The foil, copper and brass were all metals, and none of them stuck. A heavy stone did not stick either.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Finish like a scientist. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a magnet pulls only some metals. What I saw: the nail and pin stuck, but the brass key, foil and copper did not. Why: the ones that stuck must have something special inside, which is probably iron.

experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You test 16 everyday things to see which ones a magnet pulls, and look for a pattern.
