experiments.title: Through the Paper: does the pull go through things?
experiments.question: Does a magnet's pull go through other things, and how many sheets of paper can it reach through?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a magnet still pull a paper clip through a sheet of paper? Through ten sheets? Through a glass of water?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet and the same paper clip every time. Start the magnet on top of the stack each time. Change only the number of sheets. Try each stack twice.
results_table: What is between the magnet and the clip
Does the clip jump up or move?
Biggest stack of sheets where the clip still jumped

materials.item: one fridge magnet
one steel paper clip
about 30 sheets of thin paper, such as from an old notebook
a piece of cardboard, a plastic plate, a wooden ruler and a cotton cloth
a clear glass of water
a steel thali or plate

experiments.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and cards. Mop up any spilled water.

schedule.what: Test different materials between the magnet and the clip. Then count how many sheets of paper the pull can reach through.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about what happened as the stack got thicker.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper clip flat on the table. 2. Lay one sheet of paper over it. 3. Hold the magnet on the paper above the clip. 4. Slowly lift the magnet and see if the clip jumps up with it.
flow.say: Let's see if a magnet can pull a clip through a piece of paper. Put the paper over the clip, and bring the magnet down.
flow.kid: Put a paper clip on the table. Cover it with one sheet. Bring the magnet down on top. Does the clip jump?

ask.q: Did the paper stop the magnet?
good: No, the clip still jumped.
The magnet pulled right through.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Through the Paper experiment. You find out whether a magnet can pull through a sheet of paper.

flow.do: 1. Try the same with a cloth, a piece of cardboard, a plastic plate and a wooden ruler in the gap. 2. Then drag a clip up the outside of a glass of water, using the magnet on the outside. 3. Write down yes or no for each.
flow.say: Now try other things in the gap. Cloth, cardboard, plastic, wood. Then try water. Does the pull go through each one?
flow.kid: Try cloth, cardboard, plastic and wood in the gap. Then try a glass of water. Write yes or no.
flow.parent: All of these should let the pull through, unless they are very thick. The clip in the water may need to sit close to the glass wall. If it does not move, try a smaller glass.

check.q: A magnet pulls a clip through cloth, plastic and wood. What does that tell us?
options: These materials do not get in the way of the pull
The clip is made of cloth
check.why: If a thing lets the pull pass, the magnet still reaches the clip. These materials are non-magnetic. They do not grab the pull, so they do not block it. Picking 'these materials are magnetic' usually means mixing up two ideas. One is a magnet pulling through a thing. The other is a magnet pulling the thing itself.

flow.do: 1. Lay the clip on the table. 2. Stack 5 sheets over it, then bring the magnet down on top. 3. Add 5 more sheets and try again. 4. Keep adding until the clip no longer jumps. 5. Write the biggest stack where it still jumped.
flow.say: Now we find the limit. Add five sheets at a time. At some point, the clip will not jump. Write down the last stack where it did.
flow.kid: Stack 5 sheets over the clip and try the magnet. Add 5 more sheets and try again. Keep going until the clip stays put. Write the last number.
flow.parent: Many fridge magnets reach through 10 to 25 thin sheets. Weaker ones reach less. The result depends on the magnet, the paper and the clip. Your numbers may differ a lot from the example.

flow.do: 1. If you have a second, stronger magnet, repeat the stack test with it. 2. Compare the two numbers. 3. Draw a bar for each magnet.
flow.say: If you have two magnets, test both. Which one reached through more sheets? That is the stronger magnet.
flow.kid: Test a second magnet. Which one reached through more sheets? That one is stronger.

chart.title: Made-up example results: sheets of paper the pull reached through
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Test the steel thali. 1. Check whether a magnet sticks to the thali. 2. Put the clip on the other side and try to pull it with the magnet through the thali. Then say or write what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: Does the thali let the pull through? What do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Try the steel thali. Put the clip on the far side. Does the magnet pull it through? Say what, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: This depends on the steel. If your thali sticks to the magnet, it grabs the pull. The clip on the far side hardly feels it. If your thali does not stick, the pull passes through, like paper. Both results are correct. They show again that the exact steel matters.

check.q: Why does the clip stop jumping when the stack gets too thick?
options: The paper blocks the pull completely
The magnet is now too far away to pull the clip
check.why: A magnet's pull gets weaker very quickly as the gap grows. A thick stack of paper only puts the magnet further from the clip. Picking 'paper blocks it' usually means paper is imagined as a wall. But one sheet did not block it, and a stronger magnet reached through more sheets.

experiments.context: This experiment asks whether a magnet's pull goes through paper, cloth, plastic, wood and water. It also asks how far the pull can reach.

experiments.title: Lend a Nail Its Power: a magnet that can lend its pull
experiments.question: Can a magnet turn an iron nail into a magnet, and does it work for other materials?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you touch a nail to a magnet, can the nail pick up paper clips? What about an aluminium nail or a copper wire?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet and the same touch each time, for five seconds. Use objects of about the same size. Change only the material. Count the clips three times and take the middle number.
results_table: Clips it held while touching the magnet
Clips it held after the magnet moved away

materials.item: one fridge magnet
about 20 steel paper clips
an iron nail, a steel bolt or large screw, and a steel spoon
a thick piece of copper wire, a strip of aluminium foil rolled tight, and a brass key
a steel sewing needle (a grown-up handles this)

experiments.safety: A sewing needle is sharp. A grown-up does the needle step. Keep magnets away from phones and cards.

schedule.what: Hang a chain of clips from the magnet. Lend the power to different objects. Magnetise a needle.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about which materials could borrow the magnet's power.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnet up by its edge. 2. Touch one paper clip to it. 3. Touch a second clip to the first one, and a third to the second. 4. Keep going. Count how many hang in a chain.
flow.say: Let's see something odd. A paper clip is magnetic. Touch one to the magnet, then touch another clip to the first. Does it hang on?
flow.kid: Touch a paper clip to the magnet. Touch a second clip to the first. Keep going. How long can your chain be?

ask.q: The second clip does not touch the magnet. Why does it hang on?
good: The first clip became a magnet.
The magnet gave its power to the first clip.

flow.parent: Each clip in the chain becomes a weak magnet while it is near the magnet. This is the idea of the whole experiment. A chain of 3 to 6 is typical for a fridge magnet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the experiment about lending power. A magnet can turn a magnetic thing into a magnet, for a little while.

flow.do: 1. Touch the iron nail to the magnet and hold it there for five seconds. 2. Bring the loose end of the nail close to the pile of clips. 3. Count how many clips it picks up. 4. Pull the nail away from the magnet and watch the clips.
flow.say: Touch the nail to the magnet. Now see if the nail can pick up clips. Then pull the nail away from the magnet. What happens to the clips?
flow.kid: Touch a nail to the magnet. Can the nail pick up clips? Now pull the nail away. What happens?

check.q: When the nail is pulled away from the magnet, most clips fall off. What does that tell us?
options: The nail was a magnet only while the magnet was touching it
check.why: The magnet lined up the tiny magnets in the nail, so the nail could pick up clips. Without the magnet, most of them drift back out of line, and the pull fades. Picking 'the nail is not magnetic' usually means thinking that a magnetic thing must be a magnet all the time. A magnetic thing can borrow the power.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with the steel bolt, the steel spoon, the copper wire, the foil strip and the brass key. 2. For each one, touch it to the magnet for five seconds. 3. Count the clips it can pick up. 4. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now try the other things. Which ones can borrow the magnet's power? Which cannot?
flow.kid: Try the bolt, spoon, copper wire, foil and brass key. Count the clips each can pick up. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Expect clips on the nail and the bolt, and maybe a few on the steel spoon. Expect none on the copper, aluminium and brass. If your fridge magnet is weak, put the clips closer.

chart.title: Made-up example results: clips each object picked up while touching the magnet

flow.do: A grown-up does this step. 1. Hold a steel sewing needle. 2. Stroke it 30 times along one end of the magnet, always in the same direction. 3. At the end of each stroke, lift the needle away through the air. 4. Test if the needle can pick up a paper clip. 5. Do the same with an iron nail, and compare how long each keeps its pull.
flow.say: Now we try to make a lasting magnet. Stroke the needle many times in the same direction. Always lift it away at the end of each stroke.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hold the needle. Stroke it 30 times with the magnet, the same way each time. Does it pick up a clip?
flow.parent: The needle should pick up a clip or two, and keep doing it for hours or days. The nail may lose its pull quickly. Results vary a lot. Steel with more carbon keeps its magnetism better than soft iron. Scientists call that hard and soft magnetic materials.
flow.think: A fridge magnet keeps its pull for years. A nail loses it in minutes. What might be different inside?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. What I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Finish like a scientist. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: only iron-like things can borrow a magnet's power. What I saw: the nail and bolt picked up clips, but copper, foil and brass did not. Why: the nail has tiny magnets inside that the big magnet can line up. Copper and brass do not.

experiments.context: A magnet can lend some of its pull to a nail. This experiment finds out which materials can borrow it.

activities.title: Magnet Hunt at Home

materials.item: a fridge magnet
paper and a pencil, to write down what you find

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Keep the magnet away from phones, cards and the TV screen.

schedule.what: Hunt for 15 places a magnet sticks, indoors and then outside.

activities.record: Write a list of 15 places. Next to each one, write STICK or SKIP.

flow.do: Explain the hunt. Give your child the magnet, paper and pencil. Where iron comes from, ore dug out of the ground, is in the unit What Is It Made Of?
flow.say: We're magnet detectives. Let's find fifteen places where a magnet sticks, and a few where it doesn't.
flow.kid: You are a magnet detective! Find 15 places where the magnet sticks. Find a few where it does not.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnet Hunt. You walk around your home and street with a magnet, and find out where it sticks.

flow.do: Hunt around the home, then outside. Try the fridge door, almirah, pressure cooker, tawa and window grill. Outside, try a tin roof sheet, a steel gate, a cycle frame and a school bag zip.
flow.say: For each place, guess first. Then touch the magnet to it. Does it stick? Write STICK or SKIP.
flow.kid: For each place, guess first. Then test it. Write STICK or SKIP.
flow.parent: Good finds: the fridge door, steel almirah, iron gate, cycle frame, GI roofing sheet and many hinges. Surprises: the tumbler, the aluminium cooker and many zip pullers. Most modern coins are a mix, so test them. Ask which finds are painted. Paint does not stop the pull, because it is so thin.

flow.do: Ask everyone to share their most surprising find. Count the STICK places and the SKIP places.
flow.say: Which find surprised you most? Count your sticks and your skips.
flow.kid: Which find surprised you most? Count your STICK places and SKIP places.
flow.think: Why do you think so many gates, almirahs and roofs are made of iron or steel and not aluminium?

activities.title: Be the Atoms: the Domain Dance

materials.item: 3 or more people, including the grown-up
a big paper arrow, drawn on a sheet

activities.safety: Leave enough space so nobody bumps into anyone.

schedule.what: Act out wood, iron and a magnet using your arms as tiny magnets.

activities.record: Draw the three rooms: wood, iron and iron with a magnet. Show the arms as arrows.

flow.do: 1. Everyone stands in a group, a metre apart. 2. Each person holds one arm out straight like an arrow. This is a tiny magnet. 3. For wood, everyone points their arm in a different direction. 4. Walk through the group holding the big paper arrow, and see if the group moves.
flow.say: We're pretending to be the tiny magnets inside things. In wood, every arrow points a different way. Let's see what happens.
flow.kid: You are a tiny magnet inside wood. Stretch out one arm. Point it in any direction. Everyone points a different way.

ask.q: When the big arrow walks past, does the group move?
good: No, because everyone points different ways and cancels out.
The pushes and pulls cancel.

flow.parent: Say that every arrow is a tiny magnet, but together they cancel, so wood has no pull.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Domain Dance. You use your arms to act out what is going on inside wood and iron.

flow.do: 1. Now the group is iron. Split into two or three smaller groups. 2. In each small group, all arms point the same way. These are domains. 3. Different groups can point different ways. 4. Now the grown-up walks past with the big arrow. Each group slowly turns to match it.
flow.say: Now we are iron. We stand in small groups. In each group, everyone points the same way. When the big arrow comes, the groups swing round to follow it.
flow.kid: Now you are iron. Stand in a small group. Everyone in your group points the same way. When the big arrow comes, swing round to follow it.

check.q: In the dance, what makes the iron group get pulled by the big arrow?
options: The small groups turn and point the same way as the big arrow
The people in the group all point in different ways
check.why: In iron, the tiny magnets are already lined up in small groups, called domains. A magnet nearby turns the groups, so they all line up and the iron is pulled. In wood, the tiny magnets point every which way and cancel out. Picking 'different ways' describes wood, not iron.

flow.do: Talk about what the dance gets right and wrong. Then ask your child to draw the three rooms: wood, iron, and iron with a magnet.
flow.say: Real iron has trillions of atoms, not three children. And the tiny magnets are electrons, not arms. But the idea is real. Where did the dance fool us?
flow.kid: Draw three pictures: wood, iron, and iron with a magnet. Draw each tiny magnet as an arrow.
flow.think: In the dance, the groups move slowly. How do you think the groups in a real nail move so quickly?

activities.context: This is a game you act out. Your arms are the tiny magnets inside things, so you can see why iron is magnetic and wood is not.

activities.title: The Kabadiwala's Heap: sort the scrap

materials.item: a big tray or shallow box
a heap of junk, such as paper clips, safety pins, bottle caps, foil balls, rubber bands, plastic scraps and rice
a piece of copper wire, a brass key and an old steel spoon
a magnet in a clear plastic bag
three bowls or sheets of paper

activities.safety: Do not include sharp metal or broken glass. Wash hands after handling old metal.

schedule.what: Sort the mixed heap using a magnet. Then plan how to sort what is left.

activities.record: Write how many things went into each bowl. Write how you would sort the rest.

flow.do: 1. Mix everything in the tray to make a heap of scrap. 2. Ask your child to guess how many things a magnet will pull out. 3. Write the guess on the paper.
flow.say: A kabadiwala gets a huge heap of mixed scrap. How could a magnet help him? Guess how many things the magnet will pull from this heap.
flow.kid: This tray is a heap of scrap. Guess how many things the magnet will pull out. Write your number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kabadiwala's Heap. You sort a heap of mixed junk with a magnet, the way a scrap dealer does.

flow.do: 1. Move the bagged magnet just above the heap. 2. Lift off whatever sticks. 3. Pull the bag off the magnet, over a bowl marked MAGNETIC, so the things drop in. 4. Repeat until nothing else sticks.
flow.say: The magnet is the first sorter. Everything that sticks goes into the MAGNETIC bowl. The bag lets you drop them in easily.
flow.kid: Move the magnet over the heap. Everything that sticks goes into the MAGNETIC bowl. Pull the magnet out of the bag to drop them.
flow.parent: The bag keeps the magnet clean. When you pull the magnet out of the bag, the things drop. Expect clips, pins, steel caps and the steel spoon.

check.q: After the magnet is done, what is left in the tray?
options: Only things that are not iron or steel, including some metals
check.why: The magnet only takes out magnetic things. Aluminium foil, copper wire and the brass key are metals. They are left behind with the plastic and the rice. Picking 'only plastic' usually means thinking all metals are magnetic.

flow.do: 1. Look at what is left. Ask how you could separate the aluminium, copper and brass from the plastic and rice. 2. Try some ideas: tap each to hear the ring, float in water, look at the colour. 3. Put them in two or three more bowls.
flow.say: Now the magnet cannot help. How can we sort the rest? What does each thing feel, sound or look like?
flow.kid: The magnet is done. How can you sort the rest? Try colour, ringing sound, floating in water.
flow.parent: Good ideas: copper is reddish, brass is yellow, foil is silvery and bendy. Metals ring when tapped and sink in water. Plastic and rice are not shiny. This links to the Sorting Materials unit.
flow.think: In a real scrap yard, the metals worth the most are often not magnetic. Why do you think a magnet is used first?

flow.do: Talk about who does this work. Many scrap dealers and waste pickers in India sort by hand, with or without magnets.
flow.say: In many Indian cities, people sort rubbish by hand, all day, for little money. Without them, much of our metal would go to waste. Who do you think does this work for your home?
flow.kid: Who sorts rubbish for your home? Talk about it. Why is their work important?
flow.parent: Waste pickers sort a large share of India's recyclable waste. Ask the question gently, and do not make it a lecture. Many children know a kabadiwala by name.

activities.context: This is a sorting activity. You sort a mixed heap with a magnet, the way a scrap dealer does. Then you work out how to sort the rest.

activities.title: Star Dust on the Terrace

materials.item: a magnet inside a clear plastic bag, or a magnetic pick-up wand
a small tray of fine dust and grit swept from a terrace, rain gutter or drain cover
a white sheet of paper
a magnifying glass

activities.safety: A grown-up must come with you on a terrace or roof. Stay away from edges. Wash your hands after touching dust.

schedule.what: Sweep dust, drag a magnet through it, and look at what the magnet catches under a magnifying glass.

activities.record: Draw what you saw through the magnifying glass. Write how many dark specks you found.

flow.do: Tell your child the idea. 1. Tiny pieces of rock and metal fall from space every day. Some are made of iron. 2. They land everywhere, including on roofs. 3. A magnet can pick out the iron-rich ones.
flow.say: Every day, tiny bits of rock and iron fall from space onto the Earth. They are far too small to see. Some land on our roof. A magnet might catch them.
flow.kid: Tiny bits of rock and iron fall from space every day. Some may be on your roof. A magnet might catch them!
flow.context: This is the first step of Star Dust on the Terrace. You use a magnet to look for space dust in the dirt on your roof.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, sweep dust from a flat roof, a gutter or a drain cover into a tray. 2. Spread it thinly on white paper. 3. Drag the bagged magnet through it slowly. 4. Wipe whatever sticks onto a clean white sheet by pulling the magnet out of the bag.
flow.say: Drag the magnet through the dust slowly. Little dark specks will cling to the bag. Wipe them off onto the white paper.
flow.kid: Spread the dust thinly. Drag the magnet through it slowly. Little dark specks will cling to the bag. Wipe them onto white paper.
flow.parent: Expect many dark specks. Most are iron from rust flakes, vehicle brakes and welding. These look like round black beads. A tiny few may be micrometeorites. Real ones need an expert and a microscope to confirm, so be honest about that.

flow.do: 1. Look at the specks with a magnifying glass. 2. Look for round, smooth beads. 3. Draw a few. 4. Talk about where they came from.
flow.say: Look at the specks closely. Some are round like tiny balls. Where do you think they came from? Most are from Earth, some may be from space.
flow.kid: Look at the specks with the magnifying glass. Draw three of them. Where did they come from?

check.q: A magnet caught some dark specks from the roof dust. What can we be sure of?
options: They contain iron, nickel or cobalt
check.why: A magnet only pulls iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their mixtures. So the specks must contain one of these. But iron dust comes from many places, such as rust, brakes and welding. Most specks are from Earth, so we cannot be sure they come from space. Picking 'from space' usually means thinking a magnet can tell where a thing came from.

flow.think: In 2015 a musician in Norway, Jon Larsen, found real space dust on city roofs using a magnet. How might scientists check that a speck is from space?

flow.do: Talk about the finding. Real micrometeorites exist on city roofs. Scientists confirmed some in a paper in 2017.
flow.say: In 2017 scientists wrote that they had confirmed real space dust from roofs. The tiny round beads are one sign. Experts study what is inside them.
flow.kid: Real space dust has been found on roofs in cities. Experts check what is inside. Would you like to be a space dust hunter?
flow.parent: Be honest. Most of what you catch is local iron dust. The point is to see the magnet reveal a hidden crowd of iron specks. It also shows how real scientists did it.

activities.context: This activity uses a magnet to catch tiny iron specks in roof dust. It also shows how scientists found real dust from space.

activities.title: Iron for Breakfast

materials.item: a cup of breakfast cereal flakes whose box says iron has been added
a clear zip bag, or a clear glass and a spoon
warm water
a strong fridge magnet or a bar magnet wrapped in a sandwich bag
a white plate

activities.safety: Do not eat the cereal after the experiment. Keep the magnet away from phones and cards.

schedule.what: Crush cereal in water. Stir with a magnet. Look for specks of iron.

activities.record: Draw what you see on the white plate. Write whether there was iron in the cereal.

flow.do: 1. Crush a cup of cereal to a powder inside the zip bag. 2. Add warm water until it is a thin soup. 3. Let it sit for ten minutes.
flow.say: Some breakfast cereals have tiny bits of real iron added, to help our bodies. Let's see if a magnet can find them.
flow.kid: Some cereals have real iron added. Crush the cereal. Add warm water. Let it sit for ten minutes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Iron for Breakfast. You use a magnet to find the iron added to some breakfast cereals.
flow.parent: Look at the box. If it says 'iron' or 'fortified', it often has tiny iron powder added. It is safe to eat, and our stomach acid makes it usable. Not all cereals will work, and a weak magnet may find nothing.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet in the soup and stir slowly for five minutes. 2. Lift the magnet out and look at its surface. 3. Wipe it on a white plate. 4. Look closely at the tiny dark specks.
flow.say: Stir the soup slowly with the magnet. Then lift it out. Look at the surface. Are there tiny dark specks?
flow.kid: Stir slowly with the magnet for five minutes. Lift it out. Look at it. Do you see dark specks?
flow.parent: The specks look like fuzzy black dust. They are iron powder. A strong magnet helps a lot. If you find none, try a different brand or a stronger magnet.

check.q: Why did the magnet only pick up a few dark specks from the whole bowl of cereal?
options: Only the added iron is magnetic. The rest of the cereal is not
The specks were made by the magnet
check.why: Cereal is mostly grain, which is not magnetic. Only the tiny bits of iron powder added to it are pulled out. Picking 'the specks were made by the magnet' usually means thinking a magnet can change what is in a thing. It only pulls what is already there.

flow.do: Talk about iron in the body. Our blood needs a little iron to carry air around the body. Talk about where we get it: spinach, lentils, jaggery and some cereals.
flow.say: Our bodies need a tiny amount of iron to carry air in our blood. We get it from food. Which foods in our home have iron?
flow.kid: Your body needs a tiny bit of iron. Which foods have it? Lentils, jaggery, spinach.
flow.think: The iron in this cereal is a metal powder. The iron in spinach is joined into other molecules. Do you think a magnet could find that iron?

activities.context: This activity uses a magnet to find tiny specks of iron added to some breakfast cereals.

activities.title: The Mystery Bag

materials.item: an opaque cloth bag or a pillowcase
six small things: a clip, a pin, a foil ball, a cap, a peg and a steel spoon
a magnet tied to a string

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and cards. Do not put sharp things in the bag.

schedule.what: Guess what is in a bag using only a magnet on a string.

activities.record: Write what you guessed was inside, and what really was.

flow.do: 1. Without your child seeing, put the six things into the bag. 2. Close the bag. 3. Tell your child how many are inside.
flow.say: There are six things in this bag. You may not look. You may only use the magnet on a string. Can you tell which ones are magnetic?
flow.kid: Six things are in the bag. You may not look. Use the magnet on its string. Which are magnetic?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Mystery Bag. You use only a magnet to guess what is inside a bag.

flow.do: 1. Let your child hold the string and sweep the magnet around inside the bag. 2. Count how many things cling to the magnet. 3. Guess what they are. 4. Open the bag to check.
flow.say: Sweep the magnet around inside the bag. Pull it out. What clung to it? Guess what they are.
flow.kid: Sweep the magnet inside the bag. What clings to it? Guess what they are. Then look.

check.q: The magnet picked up the clip, pin and spoon, but not the other three. What do we know about the other three?
options: They are not pulled by a magnet, but we do not know what they are made of
check.why: A magnet can only say what is pulled. The foil is metal, the cap is plastic and the peg is wood. The magnet cannot tell these apart. Picking 'all plastic' or 'all wood' usually means thinking a no from the magnet names the material. It only tells us what a thing is not.

flow.do: Talk about what the magnet could and could not tell you.
flow.say: The magnet could pick out the iron things. But it could not tell us what the others were. What other test could tell us?
flow.kid: The magnet found the iron things. What other test could tell the rest apart?
flow.think: Feel, sound, shine, floating. Which test would you use to tell foil from plastic?

activities.context: This is a game of guessing. You use a magnet on a string to find out which things are hiding in a bag.

activities.title: Magnet Tag

materials.item: 3 small cards for magnetic things: a nail, a paper clip and a steel spoon
3 small cards for non-magnetic things: a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a glass bangle
a safe open space, indoors or outdoors

activities.safety: Play on a flat, clear space. No pushing. Walk fast, do not run on slippery floors.

schedule.what: Play a tag game where only magnetic things get stuck.

activities.record: Write which cards got their holders stuck, and which did not.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a face-down card. They look at it in secret. 2. One player is the MAGNET. 3. Explain the rules. If the MAGNET tags a player holding a magnetic thing, that player is STUCK and must freeze.
flow.say: One of you is the magnet. The rest of you each secretly hold a card. If the magnet tags you and your card is magnetic, you freeze. If it is not magnetic, nothing happens.
flow.kid: One player is the MAGNET. Everyone else holds a secret card. If you are tagged and your card is magnetic, you freeze!
flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Tag. It is a tag game where only the players holding magnetic things get stuck.

flow.do: 1. Play for five minutes. 2. Stuck players stay frozen until a player holding a non-magnetic card touches them. 3. After the game, everyone shows their card. 4. Swap cards and play again.
flow.say: Frozen players are freed by a friend who is holding a non-magnetic card. Play for five minutes, then show your cards.
flow.kid: Frozen? Wait for a friend with a non-magnetic card to free you. Play for five minutes, then show your cards.

ask.q: Why can a player with a wooden spoon card free a frozen player?
good: Because wood is not magnetic, so the magnet cannot stick them.
Because they are safe from the magnet.

check.q: In Magnet Tag, which card keeps you safe from the magnet?
check.why: Glass is not magnetic, so the magnet cannot catch you. The nail and the clip are both pulled by a magnet. Picking the nail usually means thinking that metal is safe because it is strong. But strong is not the same as non-magnetic.

flow.do: Talk about the game. Ask which card was safest, and which was the most risky.
flow.say: Which card was the safest to hold? Which was the riskiest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was safest? Which was most risky? Why?
flow.think: What if the steel katori card were in the game? Would it be safe or risky?

activities.context: This is a running game. One player is a magnet and tags players, but only those holding magnetic things get stuck.

activities.title: Magnet Painting

materials.item: a thick paper plate or a piece of card
poster paint in two or three colours, on a plate
a handful of steel paper clips or steel nuts
a strong fridge magnet

activities.safety: Wash hands after painting. Keep paint away from clothes. Do not put paperclips in your mouth.

schedule.what: Paint a picture by dragging a paint-covered paper clip with a magnet beneath the paper.

activities.record: Keep the painting. Write what colours you used, and what pattern the clip made.

flow.do: 1. Dip a paper clip in paint. 2. Put it on a piece of thick paper, which lies flat on a tray. 3. Ask your child to guess how they can move the clip without touching it.
flow.say: We'll paint without a brush. We'll use a magnet. The clip carries the paint. How can we move the clip without touching it?
flow.kid: Dip a paper clip in paint. Put it on the paper. How can you move it without touching it?
flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Painting. You paint a picture using a magnet under the paper to pull a paint-covered paper clip.

ask.q: Why can the magnet pull the clip through the paper?
good: The pull goes through paper.
Paper is not magnetic, so it does not block it.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnet under the paper, right below the clip. 2. Slowly move the magnet. The clip will follow, and paint a line. 3. Make spirals, swirls and zig-zags. 4. Try a different colour clip.
flow.say: Move the magnet slowly under the paper. The clip follows and draws a line. Make spirals and swirls!
flow.kid: Move the magnet slowly under the paper. The clip follows and paints. Make spirals and swirls!
flow.parent: If the clip stops moving, the paper is too thick or the magnet is too weak. Try a thinner plate or a stronger magnet.

flow.do: Let the painting dry. Talk about what happened, and why a clip painted, but a plastic cap would not.
flow.say: Why did the clip move, but a plastic button would not? Which pictures would you like to make next?
flow.kid: Why did the clip move? Would a plastic button move? Let the painting dry.
flow.think: Artists have used iron dust and magnets to make pictures for many years. What other pictures can you paint?

activities.context: This is an art activity. You use a magnet under the paper to move a paint-covered paper clip and make a painting.

projects.title: Build a Magnetic Sorting Ramp

materials.item: a stiff cardboard sheet, such as a shoebox lid, as the ramp
a stack of books to prop up the ramp
a fridge magnet or two, and sticky tape
20 steel paper clips and 20 non-magnetic bits, such as rice grains, plastic beads or paper scraps
two bowls

projects.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, cards and small children. Sweep up any dropped clips so nobody steps on them.

schedule.what: Plan your sorting ramp. Draw it. Build the first version.
Test the ramp with 20 clips mixed with 20 other bits. Count and record.
Change one thing. Test again. Compare the three designs.

projects.record: Write how many of the 20 clips your ramp caught in each test. Draw a bar for each design. Write what you changed.

flow.do: 1. Explain the task: build a ramp that sorts a mixture. 2. Ask your child to draw a plan. 3. They should show where the mixture starts, where the magnet goes, and which bowl catches what.
flow.say: Scrap yards use giant magnets to sort metal. We'll build a small sorting ramp. The things that slide down go in one bowl. The clips should stay behind.
flow.kid: Plan a sorting ramp. Draw a slope. Show where the magnet goes. Show which bowl catches what.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnetic Sorting Ramp project. You plan a ramp that uses a magnet to separate steel paper clips from rice and other bits.

flow.do: 1. Prop one end of the cardboard on a stack of books, about 20 centimetres high. 2. Tape a magnet under the middle of the ramp, so it holds the clips from below. 3. Put one bowl at the bottom to catch what slides.
flow.say: Prop up the ramp. Tape the magnet under the middle. Place a bowl at the bottom. The clips should stop at the magnet. The rice should slide down.
flow.kid: Prop up the ramp on books. Tape the magnet under the middle. Put a bowl at the bottom.
flow.parent: If the magnet is too weak, clips will slide past. If the cardboard is too thick, the pull is too far away. Both are useful things to discover.

check.q: Why does the magnet go under the ramp, not on top?
options: The pull goes through the cardboard, and the rice cannot be caught by it
The magnet would stick to the rice
check.why: The cardboard is non-magnetic, so the magnet's pull goes through it and catches the clips on top. The rice is not magnetic, so it slides on. Picking 'the magnet would stick to the rice' usually means thinking a magnet sticks to anything small. Only magnetic things stick.

flow.do: 1. Mix 20 clips with 20 non-magnetic bits. 2. Pour the mix at the top of the ramp, slowly. 3. Count how many clips stayed on the ramp and how many slid into the bowl. 4. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Pour the mixture slowly at the top. Count the clips that stayed on the ramp, and the clips that slid down. How well did your ramp work?
flow.kid: Pour the mix at the top. Count the clips that stayed. Count the clips that slid down. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Do the test in a tray to catch any bouncing clips. A typical first try catches 8 to 14 of the 20 clips. That is fine. The next step is to improve it.

flow.do: 1. Choose just ONE thing to change: the slope, the magnet, or the thickness of the card. 2. Test again with a fresh mix. 3. Count. 4. Do it a third time with a different change.
flow.say: Change just one thing. Test again. Which change catches the most clips? Change only one thing at a time, so we know what worked.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Count the clips. Do it again with a different change.

chart.title: Made-up example results: clips caught out of 20
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.think: Why must we change only one thing between tests?

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart of the three results. 2. Talk about which change helped most and why. 3. Say what you would change next.
flow.say: Which design caught the most clips? Why do you think it worked? What would you try next?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each design. Which caught the most? Why? What would you try next?
flow.parent: Good reasons: a gentler slope gives the magnet more time to grab. Two magnets pull harder or reach further. A thinner card puts the magnet closer. Notice the link to the Through the Paper experiment.

challenges.title: Rescue the Pin
challenges.problem: A steel pin has fallen into a big bowl of rice. Your job is to get it out without putting any finger in the rice, using a magnet.
constraints: You can only use a magnet and things you find at home.
The rice must stay in the bowl.
materials: a bowl of rice with a steel pin hidden in it
string, tape, a plastic bag, a spoon, a plate, a tall narrow jar
general: Put the magnet in a plastic bag. Stir it slowly through the rice. The pin clings to the bag.
Hold the magnet against the side of the bowl and move it slowly all around.
Spread the rice out on a plate, and sweep the magnet just above the surface.
creative: Tie the magnet to a string. Lower it into a tall narrow jar to rescue a pin that fell to the bottom.
Pour the rice into a tall jar. Use the magnet outside the glass to drag the pin up to the top.
Use a magnet under a plate. The pin will creep across the top of the plate, through the plate.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own rescue. Where else could a steel pin or needle get lost? Draw a place and a plan to get it back.

flow.do: 1. Hide a steel pin in a bowl of rice. 2. Ask your child to find it without putting a finger in the rice. 3. Ask for three ideas.

challenges.title: The Cupboard Door Puzzle
challenges.problem: Sunil's fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge, but it falls off the wooden cupboard door right beside it. Make a magnet stay on a wooden or plastic board, without screws or nails.
constraints: You may not use nails, screws or glue on the magnet.
The board is wood or plastic, so a magnet will not stick to it as it is.
Your fix must hold a drawing for one whole day.
materials: a wooden or plastic board, standing up
steel washers or flat steel lids
general: Stick a flat piece of steel to the board using double-sided tape. A steel washer, a thin steel lid or a steel strip all work. The magnet sticks to the steel.
Use two magnets, one on each side of a thin board, so they pull each other through the board.
Use a bigger or stronger magnet.
creative: Make a small pocket from cloth, put a steel washer inside it, and tape the pocket to the board.
Paint the board with magnetic paint. This is a real product. It has tiny iron specks mixed in, so a wall can hold magnets.
Use thin iron wire to weave a net over the board, and attach magnets to it.

opts: A magnet does not pull it, or pulls it too little to notice
quiz.why: Non-magnetic means a magnet does not pull it. Picking 'not a metal' usually means thinking that all metals are magnetic and all non-metals are not. Aluminium is a metal that is non-magnetic.

quiz.p: Mira predicts that a brass diya will stick to a magnet. She tests it and it does not. What should she do?
opts: Write down what happened and change her idea
quiz.why: A surprise is a gift in science. We write down what happened, and change our idea. Picking 'test until it sticks' usually means wanting to be right, instead of learning.

quiz.p: Why do we test each object twice with a magnet?
opts: One try could be a fluke
A magnet needs two touches to work
quiz.why: A repeat tells us whether we can trust a result. Picking 'magnets need two touches' usually means thinking a magnet needs time to charge up. It pulls at once.

quiz.p: Which metals does a magnet pull?
quiz.why: Only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic in an ordinary room. Picking 'all metals' is the most common mistake about magnets.

quiz.p: Which pair are BOTH pulled by a magnet?
opts: An iron nail and a steel paper clip
A copper wire and an iron nail
Aluminium foil and a steel pin
A brass key and a steel pin
quiz.why: The nail and the clip both contain iron. In every other pair, one of the two things is copper, aluminium or brass, which a magnet ignores.

quiz.p: Look at the table. What does it show about other metals, such as aluminium, copper and brass?
quiz.why: The table shows 0 stuck and 4 did not stick. Picking 'all of them stuck' usually means believing the idea that all metals are magnetic, before looking at the results.
quiz.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 objects with a magnet and group the results. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

quiz.p: A steel katori does not stick to a magnet, but a steel spoon does. What is the best explanation?
opts: Steel is a mixture, and the mixtures differ
quiz.why: Steel is an alloy. Some steels have a lot of nickel, which stops the pull. Picking 'plastic' usually means thinking a thing that does not stick cannot be metal.
Brass is copper and zinc. Steel is iron and carbon. Bronze is copper and tin. All the metals in brass are non-magnetic, so brass is not magnetic.

quiz.p: A magnet pulls a paper clip through a sheet of paper. What does this show?
opts: Paper does not block the pull
quiz.why: Non-magnetic materials like paper let the pull pass. Picking 'paper is magnetic' usually means mixing up two things. One lets the pull through. The other is itself pulled.

quiz.p: A clip stops jumping when 40 sheets of paper are between it and the magnet. Why?
opts: The magnet is too far away to pull the clip
quiz.why: A magnet's pull gets weaker quickly as the gap grows. The thick stack does not block the pull. It makes the gap big.

quiz.p: A magnet sticks to a gold-coloured chain. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.why: Gold is not magnetic. So a chain that sticks must have a magnetic metal in it, and it cannot be pure gold. Picking 'pure gold' usually means thinking that a stronger pull means a better metal.

quiz.p: A key does not stick to a magnet. Which is the best thing to say?
opts: It might be brass, aluminium, copper or a steel that does not stick. We cannot tell which
quiz.why: A magnet can only say what is pulled. Many different metals are not pulled, so a no tells us little. A magnet is best at saying yes to iron, nickel and cobalt.

quiz.p: How does a scrap dealer use a magnet?
opts: To pull iron and steel out of a mixed heap
quiz.why: A big magnet lifts iron and steel and leaves the rest. Aluminium, copper and brass, which are worth more, are sorted by other tests.

opts: Tiny magnets inside it line up in groups called domains
quiz.why: In iron, the tiny magnets from electrons line up in patches. A nearby magnet turns the patches, so the iron is pulled. Picking 'shiny' or 'heavy' usually means choosing something we can see, instead of something inside.

quiz.p: What do scientists think makes the Earth's magnetic field?
opts: Flowing liquid iron in the outer core
A giant bar magnet at the centre
quiz.why: The core is too hot to be a permanent magnet. Scientists think flowing liquid iron makes the field. Picking 'a giant bar magnet' is a common picture in old books.

quiz.p: Why does a red-hot iron nail not stick to a magnet?
opts: Heat jiggles the atoms so much that the tiny magnets cannot line up
quiz.why: Above its Curie point of about 770 degrees Celsius, iron is not magnetic. Cool it down and it is magnetic again.

Loudspeakers and headphones use a magnet and a coil to turn electric signals into sound.
Electric fans, mixer grinders and car motors have magnets or electromagnets inside them.

A compass needle is a small magnet that points north.
Old cassette tapes, and the stripe on some cards, store information in tiny magnetic particles.
Hospitals use huge magnets in MRI scanners to look inside the body without cutting.
Magnetic whiteboards and notice boards hold papers with small magnets.
Maglev trains in Japan and China float above the track on magnets and travel without wheels touching.
Mining companies use magnets to separate iron ore from other rock.
Pencil boxes and school bags often close with a small magnet and a steel plate.

open_questions.q: Can scientists predict which new mixtures of metals will be magnetic?
open_questions.why_open: Often they can only guess. Computers are getting better at it, but surprises such as Heusler's alloy still happen.

open_questions.q: How do birds, turtles and fish sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have shown that they can, but not how. Ideas include tiny crystals of magnetite, and a light-sensitive protein in the eye.

open_questions.q: Why does the Earth's magnetic field flip, with north and south swapping places?
open_questions.why_open: Rocks show that it has flipped hundreds of times. The last big flip was about 780,000 years ago. Nobody knows exactly why, or when the next one will be.

open_questions.q: When did the Earth's solid inner core form?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates range from about half a billion to well over a billion years ago. It is very hard to find out, since the core is thousands of kilometres down.

open_questions.q: Can we make strong magnets without rare earth metals such as neodymium?
open_questions.why_open: Rare earths are hard to mine and clean, and are found in only a few places. Scientists are trying to find strong magnets made from more common metals, but have not yet matched neodymium.

open_questions.q: Can a magnet be made from carbon and other light elements, with no metal?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made magnets from molecules. Most work only when very cold. A cheap, strong one that works in a kitchen would be a surprise.

open_questions.q: Can humans sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: In 2019 a team in California found that human brain waves changed when the magnetic field around people was turned. Other scientists want the result checked again and again.

open_questions.q: Why are only iron, nickel and cobalt magnetic in a room, when many metals have electrons that could line up?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics can explain it for each metal after it is measured. But predicting it from scratch for a new material is still very difficult.

maths.problem: In the lending experiment, the iron nail picked up 6 clips. The steel bolt picked up 5, the steel spoon 2 and the copper wire 0. Draw a bar chart of these. How many more clips did the nail pick up than the spoon?
maths.answer: 4 more clips. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each object, as tall as its number of clips. The nail's bar is 6 tall and the spoon's is 2 tall. To find how many more, take away: 6 minus 2 is 4. You can check: 2 and 4 more makes 6.
maths.context: In the lending experiment, you touch objects to a magnet and count the paper clips each one can pick up. Here are some made-up results.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example results: clips each object picked up while touching the magnet

maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart makes the best result jump out, and subtracting tells us by how much.

maths.problem: In the Great Magnet Test, 16 objects were tested. 6 of them stuck to the magnet. How many did not stick?
maths.explain: There were 16 objects in all, and 6 of them stuck. The rest did not stick. 16 take away 6 is 10. You can check: 10 and 6 make 16.
maths.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 everyday objects with a magnet. You sort them into those that stick and those that do not.
maths.why_maths: Scientists count both groups: what happened and what did not. Subtracting gives the second count without testing again.

maths.problem: Out of 12 objects, 3 stuck to the magnet. What fraction of the objects stuck? Say it in words.
maths.answer: One quarter of the objects stuck.
maths.explain: Share the 12 objects into 4 equal groups, and each group has 3 objects. So the 3 objects that stuck make one of the 4 equal groups. That is one quarter. You can check: 4 groups of 3 make 12.
maths.context: In a magnet test, you sort objects into those that stick and those that do not. Here are some made-up results for 12 objects.
maths.why_maths: Fractions tell us how big one group is compared with the whole. 'One quarter stuck' is easier to remember and to compare than '3 out of 12'.

maths.problem: A sorting ramp has 4 magnets. Each magnet catches 6 clips. How many clips does the ramp catch in all?
maths.explain: There are 4 groups of 6 clips. Add them up: 6 and 6 is 12. 12 and 6 is 18. 18 and 6 is 24. Or use the tables: 4 times 6 is 24.
maths.context: In the Magnetic Sorting Ramp project, you build a ramp with a magnet underneath to catch steel paper clips. This question imagines a ramp with 4 magnets.
maths.why_maths: Engineers often add up equal groups, such as clips per magnet. Multiplying is a fast way to do it.

maths.problem: A stack of paper that a magnet reached through is measured with a ruler, as shown. How thick is the stack?
maths.explain: The top of the stack lines up halfway between the 3 and the 4. Each small mark on the ruler is half a centimetre. So the stack is 3 centimetres and half a centimetre more. That is 3 and a half centimetres.
maths.context: In the Through the Paper experiment, you stack paper sheets between a magnet and a paper clip. To compare two magnets, you need to measure how thick the stack is.

answer_chart.title: A ruler, measuring in centimetres (cm)
answer_chart.label: Each small mark is half a centimetre.

maths.why_maths: A ruler only helps if you can read it. Reading the small marks turns a stack of paper into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: A kabadiwala pays 25 rupees for each kilogram of iron scrap. This price is made up. Hira sells 4 kilograms of iron scrap that she sorted with a magnet. How many rupees does she get?
maths.explain: She gets 25 rupees for each of 4 kilograms. That is 4 groups of 25. 25 and 25 is 50. 50 and 25 is 75. 75 and 25 is 100. So she gets 100 rupees.
maths.context: In The Kabadiwala's Heap, you sort a heap of scrap with a magnet. Scrap dealers pay for scrap by its weight. The price in this question is made up.
maths.why_maths: Sorting with a magnet is only useful because each kind of metal has a price. Multiplying weight by price tells us what the sorted metal is worth.

maths.problem: William Gilbert wrote his book about magnets in 1600. Pierre Curie measured how heat changes magnets in 1895. How many years later was Curie's work?
maths.explain: Take 1600 away from 1895. 1895 minus 1600 is 295. You can check: 1600 and 295 make 1895.
maths.context: People have been studying magnets for a very long time. William Gilbert wrote a famous book in 1600. Pierre Curie found out what heat does to a magnet in 1895.
maths.why_maths: Taking one year away from another tells us how much time lies between two discoveries. It shows how slowly science can grow.

roots.context: We have been learning that a magnet picks some things and leaves others. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves, about life, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: An invisible pull reaches through empty space and through paper.
deep_truth.habit: We think things must touch to affect each other. A magnet moves a pin through a page without touching it.
deep_truth.evidence: A magnet pulls a paper clip through a book cover.

three.who_am_i: You are made of atoms, and each atom has tiny spinning magnets inside. Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star.
three.what_is_life: Life uses magnets too. Some bacteria carry a chain of tiny magnets as a compass, and many animals can feel the Earth's magnetic pull.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of pulls we cannot see. A magnet reaches across a gap and holds a nail, with nothing in between that our eyes can find.

roots.thread: Every electron is a tiny magnet. In wood, copper and brass, the tiny magnets point every which way. They cancel out to nothing, like the zero DeepKids talks about. In iron, nickel and cobalt, the tiny magnets agree, and the many become one big pull. DeepKids believes this is how the One shows up as the many all through the world. Zero holds everything in balance, and when many parts turn together, something new appears. A nail is a crowd that has learned to lean the same way.

teachings.teaching: A teacher, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water and come back in the morning. The salt cannot be seen, but it is in every sip. The teacher says that what is unseen can be the very heart of things.
teachings.link: A magnet's pull is unseen, yet it fills the space around the magnet and holds the nail. The salt and the magnet both show that what we cannot see can be everywhere.

teachings.link: In a nail, each tiny magnet leans towards its neighbours, and every neighbour leans back. Each one is shaped by all of the others, like the jewels.

teachings.source: Aristotle, On the Soul 405a, reporting Thales of Miletus
teachings.teaching: Thales said that a lodestone has a soul, because it moves iron. He was among the first to look for a reason inside nature itself.
teachings.link: We now explain the pull with electrons and fields. The wonder Thales felt is still here. You feel it when a fridge magnet moves a clip with no hand.

science.text: Every electron acts like a tiny magnet. In most materials the tiny magnets cancel out. In iron, nickel and cobalt they line up in groups.
Scientists do not yet agree on how birds feel the Earth's magnetic field. One idea uses tiny magnets in the body, and another uses a light-sensitive protein in the eye.

other_view.who: Many physicists, and the Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: When we say the tiny magnets agree, we are using a human word for a rule of physics. Electrons line up because of laws of quantum physics, and there is nothing like a mind in a nail. The Charvaka thinkers taught that there is only matter, and that we should trust only what we can perceive.

practice.title: The gap between your hands
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Hold your hands out in front of you, palms facing each other, about a hand's width apart. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. Now move your hands a little closer, and a little further. Notice anything between them. Some people feel warmth or a tingle. That is your own blood and attention, and it is not magnetism. But notice that you can feel something reaching across a gap. Open your eyes. Is the gap empty?
practice.kid: Hold your hands out, palms facing, and close your eyes. Breathe slowly while you move them closer and further. What do you feel in the gap? Is it really empty?

ask: When many tiny things all lean the same way, they can pull something big. Where have you seen people do this?
A magnet's pull crosses a gap with nothing in it that you can see. What else do you feel but cannot see?
If every tiny magnet in a nail is a small part of one big pull, which part is the nail? Where does the pull begin?
